title: Mathematical Foundations of Algorithms
description: A comprehensive multiple-choice question bank covering mathematical foundations of computer algorithms, algorithm analysis, complexity, recursion, recurrence relations, graph theory, searching, combinatorics, and runtime modeling.

questions.concept: Computing throughput from total items and elapsed time
questions.learningObjective: Compute throughput as items processed divided by elapsed time.
questions.question: A pipeline processes \(900\) documents in \(4\) seconds at a steady rate. What is its throughput in documents per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput is the number of processed items divided by elapsed time: \(\frac{900}{4}=225\) documents per second.
questions.hint: Divide the total number of processed items by the elapsed time.

questions.concept: Counting edges in a complete graph
questions.learningObjective: Count the unordered vertex pairs of a simple undirected complete graph.
questions.question: How many edges are in a simple undirected complete graph with \(n=22\) vertices?
questions.explanation: Each edge joins one unordered pair of distinct vertices. Therefore, \(\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\). Substituting \(n=22\) gives \(\frac{22\cdot 21}{2}=231\).
questions.hint: Count unordered pairs of distinct vertices.

questions.concept: Solving the characteristic equation of a linear recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Solve a quadratic characteristic equation associated with a linear recurrence relation.
questions.question: A linear recurrence has the characteristic equation \(x^2-4=0\). What are its two roots?
questions.explanation:
Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2-4&=(x+2)(x-2)\\
(x+2)(x-2)&=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-2\) and \(x=2\). Their sum is \(-2+2=0\) and their product is \((-2)(2)=-4\), matching the coefficients.
questions.hint: Find a pair whose sum is the negative of the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

questions.concept: Applying the tree edge-count property
questions.learningObjective: Use the edge-count property of a finite tree.
questions.question: A spanning tree connects \(n=30\) vertices of a connected undirected network. How many edges does the tree contain?
questions.explanation: A tree with \(n\) vertices has exactly \(n-1\) edges. Starting with one root, each of the remaining vertices adds one edge to its parent. Here, \(30-1=29\).
questions.hint: In a tree, each vertex other than the root has one edge to its parent.

questions.concept: Computing a net workload reduction (delta)
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a net change (delta) between two workload measurements, including its direction.
questions.question: Caching reduces a service's operation count from \(808\) to \(672\) operations per request. By how many operations per request does the count decrease?
questions.explanation: The reduction is the original count minus the new count: \(808-672=136\) operations per request. This positive reduction measures the size of the decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the new count from the original count.

questions.concept: Solving a simple additive recurrence by unrolling
questions.learningObjective: Solve a linear recurrence with a fixed additive increment by unrolling it to the base case.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers \(n\), a recurrence satisfies \(T(n)=T(n-1)+4\) for \(n\ge 1\), with \(T(0)=4\). What is \(T(8)\)?
questions.explanation: There are \(8\) steps from the base case, and each adds \(4\). Therefore, \(T(8)=4+8\cdot 4=36\).
questions.hint: Count the steps from the base case and add the increment once per step.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for binary search
questions.learningObjective: Count worst-case key-to-element comparisons in a specified standard binary-search implementation.
questions.question: Standard binary search examines a sorted array of \(n=512\) distinct elements. It uses an inclusive index interval, chooses the lower middle index, and removes the middle element after an unequal comparison. Count one three-way key-to-element comparison per examined element; exclude index and loop-condition checks. What is the maximum number of these comparisons over all present or absent targets?
questions.explanation: The worst remaining interval after one comparison has \(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor\) elements. Hence \(C(0)=0\) and \(C(n)=1+C(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor)\) for \(n\ge 1\). Repeated halving until the interval is empty gives \(C(n)=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\). For this array, \(C(512)=\lfloor\log_2 512\rfloor+1=10\).
questions.hint: Include the comparison with the final remaining element; stopping when only one candidate remains can miss a comparison.

questions.concept: Computing total base-case work across a recursion tree
questions.learningObjective: Combine subproblem count and per-subproblem cost to find total work at the base-case level.
questions.question: A divide-and-conquer algorithm starts with input size \(n=32\). Each non-base call makes \(2\) recursive calls on inputs of half its size. The root is depth \(0\), and all calls reach the base case at depth \(5\), with input size \(1\). Each base-case call performs \(6\) operations. How many operations are performed by all base-case calls combined?
questions.explanation: Each branching level multiplies the number of calls by \(2\). Thus there are \(2^{5}=32\) leaves, and their combined work is \(32\cdot 6=192\) operations.
questions.hint: Count the leaves first, then multiply by the work done at each leaf.

questions.concept: Solving the characteristic equation of a linear recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Solve a quadratic characteristic equation associated with a linear recurrence relation.
questions.question: A linear recurrence has the characteristic equation \(x^2-3x-10=0\). What are its two roots?
questions.explanation:
Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2-3x-10&=(x+2)(x-5)\\
(x+2)(x-5)&=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-2\) and \(x=5\). Their sum is \(-2+5=3\) and their product is \((-2)(5)=-10\), matching the coefficients.
questions.hint: Find a pair whose sum is the negative of the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

questions.question: Caching reduces a service's operation count from \(788\) to \(183\) operations per request. By how many operations per request does the count decrease?

questions.question: For nonnegative integers \(n\), a recurrence satisfies \(T(n)=T(n-1)+8\) for \(n\ge 1\), with \(T(0)=5\). What is \(T(8)\)?
questions.explanation: There are \(8\) steps from the base case, and each adds \(8\). Therefore, \(T(8)=5+8\cdot 8=69\).

questions.concept: Identifying the complexity class of a quadratic model
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tight asymptotic class of a quadratic operation-count model.
questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=4n^2+6n+20\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n^2}=4+\frac{6}{n}+\frac{20}{n^2}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(4\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n^2)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.
questions.hint: Identify the highest power with a nonzero positive coefficient.

questions.concept: Computing a value modulo m for hash bucket assignment
questions.learningObjective: Apply the modulo operation to compute a hash bucket index.
questions.question: A hash table assigns key \(131\) to bucket \(131\bmod 5\). What is the bucket index, using remainders from \(0\) through \(4\)?
questions.explanation: Euclidean division gives \(131=5\cdot 26+1\). Since \(0\le 1<5\), the remainder and bucket index are \(1\).
questions.hint: Use the remainder, rather than the quotient, after division by the bucket count.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on quadratic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a quadratic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=9n^2\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(3\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?
questions.explanation:
Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T(3n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{9(3n)^2}{9n^2}\\
&=3^2=9
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(9\).
questions.hint: Substitute the scaled input and form the ratio of the new model to the original.

questions.concept: Break-even input size between two algorithms
questions.learningObjective: Find the input size at which two linear-time algorithms perform the same number of operations.
questions.question: Algorithm A uses \(7n+5\) operations and Algorithm B uses \(4n+14\) operations for input size \(n\). At which nonnegative integer input size do the counts agree?
questions.explanation:
Set the operation counts equal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
7n+5&=4n+14\\
3n&=9\\
n&=3
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution gives \(7(3)+5=26\) for A and \(4(3)+14=26\) for B.
questions.hint: Equate the two expressions and collect the terms containing the input size.

questions.concept: Counting steps in the Euclidean algorithm
questions.learningObjective: Trace the Euclidean algorithm to count the number of division steps to compute a GCD.
questions.question: Starting with \((133,68)\), run the Euclidean algorithm to compute \(\gcd(133,68)\). Count every remainder-producing division, including the final division whose remainder is zero. How many division steps are required?
questions.explanation:
The divisions are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
133&=1\cdot 68+65\\
68&=1\cdot 65+3\\
65&=21\cdot 3+2\\
3&=1\cdot 2+1\\
2&=2\cdot 1+0
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(5\) divisions, including the final zero-remainder division. The last nonzero remainder (or divisor at termination) is \(1\), the greatest common divisor.
questions.hint: Record one step for each computed remainder, and include the step that produces zero.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for linear search
questions.learningObjective: Recall the worst-case comparison count for a linear search over n elements.
questions.question: Linear search checks an unsorted array of \(n=448\) elements one at a time. Count one equality comparison between the target and each examined element. What is the worst-case comparison count when the target may be present or absent?
questions.explanation: If the target is absent, every element must be checked. If it is last, the same number of checks is needed. Thus the maximum is \(n=448\) key-to-element comparisons.
questions.hint: Consider a target that is absent or is the final element checked.

questions.concept: Computing a term of a geometric sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute a requested term from the first term and common ratio of a geometric sequence.
questions.question: A geometric sequence has \(a_1=5\) and common ratio \(3\). What is \(a_{6}\)?
questions.explanation: The first term is multiplied by the common ratio \(5\) times to reach term \(6\): \(a_{6}=5\cdot 3^{5}=1215\).
questions.hint: The exponent is one less than the index of the requested term.

questions.concept: Applying the pigeonhole principle to guarantee a minimum bin size
questions.learningObjective: Apply the pigeonhole principle's ceiling-division bound.
questions.question: \(12\) items are distributed among \(10\) labeled bins. What is the largest integer \(L\) such that every distribution guarantees at least one bin containing \(L\) or more items?
questions.explanation: If every bin held at most \(1\) items, the total would be at most \(10\cdot 1=10\), which is less than \(12\). Therefore some bin has at least \(\left\lceil\frac{12}{10}\right\rceil=2\) items. Distributing the items as evenly as possible attains this largest-bin size, so no stronger guarantee is possible.
questions.hint: Find the ceiling of the average bin size, then check an even distribution to see whether the bound is sharp.

questions.concept: Applying a proportional scale factor to a workload
questions.learningObjective: Apply a proportional scale factor directly to a workload quantity.
questions.question: A model's workload is directly proportional to input size. The current workload is \(7\) operations. If the input size is multiplied by \(2\), what is the new workload?
questions.explanation: Direct proportionality applies the same factor to the workload: \(7\cdot 2=14\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply the original workload by the input-size scale factor.

questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n^2}=4+\frac{8}{n}+\frac{4}{n^2}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(4\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n^2)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.

questions.concept: Expressing a workload change as a signed delta
questions.learningObjective: Correctly interpret a negative signed delta as a decrease, distinct from a negative operation count.
questions.question: A refactor changes a function's operation count from \(158\) to \(12\) operations per call. Define the signed change as \(\Delta=\text{new}-\text{original}\). What is \(\Delta\)?
questions.explanation: Using the specified sign convention, \(\Delta=12-158=-146\) operations per call. The negative sign denotes a decrease; the new operation count itself is \(12\) and remains nonnegative.
questions.hint: Use the stated order of subtraction, and let the sign show the direction of change.

questions.concept: Determining whether a number is prime
questions.learningObjective: Determine primality by checking for divisors up to the square root of the number.
questions.question: Which statement correctly classifies the integer \(87\) as prime or composite?

options.label: B
options.text: Prime: its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(87\).

questions.explanation: The number has a nontrivial divisor: \(87=3\cdot 29\). Both factors exceed \(1\), so the number is composite.
questions.hint: Try divisors up to the square root; one nontrivial divisor is enough to prove compositeness.

questions.concept: Applying the Master Theorem to classify a recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Apply the Master Theorem, including the regularity condition when needed, without rounding critical exponents.
questions.question: For \(n=3^k\) with nonnegative integer \(k\), suppose \(T(1)=1\) and \(T(n)=4T\!\left(\frac{n}{3}\right)+n^2\) for \(n>1\). Which Master Theorem case and tight asymptotic bound apply?
questions.explanation: Because \(4<3^{2}\), \(2>\log_{3}4\). Thus the combine cost is polynomially larger than the critical term. The regularity condition holds: \(a f(\frac{n}{b})=\frac{4}{3^{2}}f(n)\), with \(c=\frac{4}{3^{2}}<1\). Therefore Case \(3\) gives \(T(n)=\Theta(n^2)\).
questions.hint: Compare the branching factor with the shrink factor raised to the combine-cost exponent; for combine-cost dominance, also check regularity.

questions.concept: Applying the handshake lemma to count edges from vertex degrees
questions.learningObjective: Use the handshake lemma on a realizable simple undirected graph.
questions.question: A simple undirected graph has \(9\) vertices with degree sequence \((3,4,6,5,1,6,1,7,3)\). How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: Each edge contributes one degree at each of its two endpoints. The degree sum is \(3+4+6+5+1+6+1+7+3=36\), so \(|E|=\frac{36}{2}=18\). The listed sequence has an explicit simple-graph realization, so this degree sum corresponds to a possible graph.
questions.hint: Count how often each edge is included when you add all vertex degrees.

questions.concept: Computing expected trials until first success (geometric distribution)
questions.learningObjective: Compute the expected number of independent trials up to and including the first success.
questions.question: An algorithm succeeds on each attempt independently with the same probability \(p=\frac{1}{16}\). Let \(X\) count all attempts up to and including the first success. What is \(\mathbb{E}[X]\)?
questions.explanation: One attempt is always made. With probability \(1-p\), a failure leaves the same expected number of additional attempts. Thus \(\mathbb{E}[X]=1+(1-p)\mathbb{E}[X]\), which gives \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{1}{p}=16\). The first successful attempt is included.
questions.hint: After a failed attempt, the remaining task has the same distribution as at the start.

questions.concept: Counting leaves in a recursion tree
questions.learningObjective: Count the number of base-case invocations in a recursion tree with a fixed branching factor and depth.
questions.question: The root call is at depth \(0\). Every call at a depth less than \(5\) makes exactly \(4\) child calls, and all calls at depth \(5\) are base cases. How many base-case calls are made?
questions.explanation: The number of calls starts at \(1\) and is multiplied by \(4\) at each depth. At depth \(5\), the leaf count is \(4^{5}=1024\).
questions.hint: Count one branching multiplication for each edge-depth between the root and a leaf.

questions.concept: Break-even input size between two algorithms
questions.learningObjective: Find the input size at which two linear-time algorithms perform the same number of operations.
questions.question: Algorithm A uses \(9n+12\) operations and Algorithm B uses \(7n+44\) operations for input size \(n\). At which nonnegative integer input size do the counts agree?
questions.explanation:
Set the operation counts equal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
9n+12&=7n+44\\
2n&=32\\
n&=16
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution gives \(9(16)+12=156\) for A and \(7(16)+44=156\) for B.
questions.hint: Equate the two expressions and collect the terms containing the input size.

questions.concept: Computing terms of a Fibonacci-style recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Compute terms of a two-term linear recurrence by direct iteration.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers, \(a_0=3\) and \(a_1=3\), while \(a_k=a_{k-1}+a_{k-2}\) for \(k\ge 2\). What is \(a_{5}\)?
questions.explanation:
Build each term from the previous two:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2}&=3+3=6\\
a_{3}&=6+3=9\\
a_{4}&=9+6=15\\
a_{5}&=15+9=24
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(a_{5}=24\).
questions.hint: Start from the two given initial values and compute one new term at a time.

questions.concept: Summing sequential pipeline stage runtimes
questions.learningObjective: Sum the runtimes of sequential pipeline stages to find total processing time.
questions.question: One item passes through \(5\) sequential pipeline stages taking \(25\), \(5\), \(10\), \(4\), \(7\) milliseconds, respectively. The item incurs no other delay, and its stages do not overlap. What is its total processing time?
questions.explanation: Add the sequential stage durations: \(25+5+10+4+7=51\) milliseconds.
questions.hint: The same item completes each stage before starting the next.

questions.concept: Bounding the length of a shortest simple path
questions.learningObjective: Prove and attain the largest possible shortest-path distance in a simple connected unweighted graph.
questions.question: Consider all simple connected undirected unweighted graphs on \(n=6\) vertices and all pairs of distinct vertices in them. What is the largest possible shortest-path length, measured in edges?
questions.explanation: A shortest path cannot repeat a vertex: removing a cycle would shorten it. It therefore visits at most \(6\) vertices and uses at most \(n-1=5\) edges. This bound is achieved by the two endpoints of a path graph on \(6\) vertices, so it is the largest possible value.
questions.hint: Use the no-repeated-vertex bound, then consider the endpoints of a graph that is itself a path.

questions.concept: Counting permutations of a set of distinct items
questions.learningObjective: Recall and apply the factorial formula for counting permutations.
questions.question: An algorithm considers every ordering of \(5\) distinct servers. How many orderings are possible?
questions.explanation: There are \(5\) choices for the first position, \(4\) for the next, and so on. The product is \(5!=\prod_{i=1}^{5}i=120\).
questions.hint: Use the multiplication principle with one fewer available item at each new position.

questions.concept: Computing terms of a Fibonacci-style recurrence

questions.question: For nonnegative integers, \(a_0=2\) and \(a_1=1\), while \(a_k=a_{k-1}+a_{k-2}\) for \(k\ge 2\). What is \(a_{6}\)?

Build each term from the previous two:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2}&=1+2=3\\
a_{3}&=3+1=4\\
a_{4}&=4+3=7\\
a_{5}&=7+4=11\\
a_{6}&=11+7=18
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(a_{6}=18\).
questions.hint: Start from the two given initial values and compute one new term at a time.

questions.concept: Applying the tree edge-count property

questions.question: A spanning tree connects \(n=55\) vertices of a connected undirected network. How many edges does the tree contain?
questions.explanation: A tree with \(n\) vertices has exactly \(n-1\) edges. Starting with one root, each of the remaining vertices adds one edge to its parent. Here, \(55-1=54\).

questions.concept: Solving a shared-workload equation with algebraic fractions
questions.learningObjective: Clear algebraic fractions to solve for a total workload split across two processes.
questions.question: A workload contains \(n\) items. In one round, two processes handle disjoint parts: the first processes \(\frac{n}{5}\) items and the second processes \(\frac{n}{6}\) items. Together they process \(66\) items in that round; the rest remain for later. What is the total workload \(n\)?
questions.explanation:
Add the two disjoint processed parts:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{n}{5}+\frac{n}{6}&=66\\
11n&=1980\\
n&=180
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution gives \(36\) items for the first process and \(30\) for the second, totaling \(66\).
questions.hint: Add the two fractional portions, then clear the denominators.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=1000000\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the smallest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the smallest expression is \(n\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Interpreting an amortized cost bound
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what an amortized per-operation bound implies about total cost over many operations.
questions.question: Starting from an empty dynamic array, a resizing policy guarantees that the total number of element-copy operations over \(21\) insertions is at most \(5\) times the number of insertions. What is the smallest total upper bound supplied by this guarantee alone?
questions.explanation: Apply the given aggregate guarantee: \(5\cdot 21=105\) element-copy operations. This is an upper bound on the entire sequence; an individual insertion may copy more than \(5\) elements.
questions.hint: Apply the stated bound to the entire insertion sequence, rather than to one worst-case insertion.

questions.concept: Evaluating a linear operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a linear time-complexity model with a fixed cost and a per-element cost for a given input size.
questions.question: An algorithm has the exact operation-count model \(T(n)=8n+28\). How many operations does it perform when \(n=14\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute the input size: \(T(14)=8\cdot 14+28=140\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply by the per-element coefficient, then add the fixed overhead.

questions.concept: Evaluating a linear operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a linear time-complexity model with a fixed cost and a per-element cost for a given input size.
questions.question: An algorithm has the exact operation-count model \(T(n)=7n+12\). How many operations does it perform when \(n=15\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute the input size: \(T(15)=7\cdot 15+12=117\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply by the per-element coefficient, then add the fixed overhead.

questions.concept: Counting nodes discovered at a given BFS layer
questions.learningObjective: Count nodes at a given BFS layer in a uniformly branching tree.
questions.question: Breadth-first search explores a rooted tree through layer \(2\). The root is layer \(0\), and every vertex in an earlier layer has exactly \(4\) distinct children. How many vertices are in layer \(2\)?
questions.explanation: A tree gives every child exactly one parent, so no vertices are shared between branches. The layer size is multiplied by \(4\) at each step, giving \(4^{2}=16\) vertices.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of vertices by the branching factor once per layer.

questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a quadratic time-complexity model with quadratic, linear, and constant terms for a given input size.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=n^2+3n+8\). How many operations are performed when \(n=5\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute and compute the square first:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(5)&=1\cdot 5^2+3\cdot 5+8\\
&=25+15+8=48
\end{aligned}
\]
The count is \(48\) operations.
questions.hint: Square the input size before multiplying by the leading coefficient.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on cubic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a cubic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=8n^3\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(2\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?
questions.explanation:
Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T(2n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{8(2n)^3}{8n^3}\\
&=2^3=8
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(8\).
questions.hint: Substitute the scaled input and form the ratio of the new model to the original.

questions.concept: Applying the tree edge-count property
questions.learningObjective: Use the edge-count property of a finite tree.
questions.question: A spanning tree connects \(n=92\) vertices of a connected undirected network. How many edges does the tree contain?
questions.explanation: A tree with \(n\) vertices has exactly \(n-1\) edges. Starting with one root, each of the remaining vertices adds one edge to its parent. Here, \(92-1=91\).
questions.hint: In a tree, each vertex other than the root has one edge to its parent.

questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a quadratic time-complexity model with quadratic, linear, and constant terms for a given input size.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=n^2+2n+14\). How many operations are performed when \(n=4\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute and compute the square first:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(4)&=1\cdot 4^2+2\cdot 4+14\\
&=16+8+14=38
\end{aligned}
\]
The count is \(38\) operations.
questions.hint: Square the input size before multiplying by the leading coefficient.

questions.concept: Computing geometric growth over repeated rounds
questions.learningObjective: Apply the geometric growth repeated-multiplication model.
questions.question: A crawler starts with \(25\) discovered pages at round \(0\). Its discovered-page count is multiplied by \(3\) at the end of every round. How many pages are counted after \(5\) rounds?
questions.explanation: The growth factor is applied once per round: \(25\cdot 3^{5}=25\cdot 243=6075\) pages.
questions.hint: Use one multiplication by the growth factor for each completed round.

questions.concept: Interpreting an amortized cost bound
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what an amortized per-operation bound implies about total cost over many operations.
questions.question: Starting from an empty dynamic array, a resizing policy guarantees that the total number of element-copy operations over \(56\) insertions is at most \(5\) times the number of insertions. What is the smallest total upper bound supplied by this guarantee alone?
questions.explanation: Apply the given aggregate guarantee: \(5\cdot 56=280\) element-copy operations. This is an upper bound on the entire sequence; an individual insertion may copy more than \(5\) elements.
questions.hint: Apply the stated bound to the entire insertion sequence, rather than to one worst-case insertion.

questions.concept: Inverse proportional scaling of time with number of workers
questions.learningObjective: Solve an inverse-proportion problem relating completion time to the number of parallel workers.
questions.question: A fixed job takes \(38\) minutes with \(6\) identical workers. Assume all work is perfectly divisible, all workers run at the same constant rate, and there is no communication, setup, or sequential overhead. How long does the job take with \(4\) workers?
questions.explanation: The required worker-time is fixed: \(6\cdot 38=228\) worker-minutes. Dividing by the new worker count gives \(\frac{228}{4}=57\) minutes.
questions.hint: Keep the product of the worker count and completion time constant.

questions.concept: Computing a net workload reduction (delta)
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a net change (delta) between two workload measurements, including its direction.
questions.question: Caching reduces a service's operation count from \(165\) to \(67\) operations per request. By how many operations per request does the count decrease?
questions.explanation: The reduction is the original count minus the new count: \(165-67=98\) operations per request. This positive reduction measures the size of the decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the new count from the original count.

questions.concept: Computing a term of a geometric sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute a requested term from the first term and common ratio of a geometric sequence.
questions.question: A geometric sequence has \(a_1=2\) and common ratio \(2\). What is \(a_{5}\)?
questions.explanation: The first term is multiplied by the common ratio \(4\) times to reach term \(5\): \(a_{5}=2\cdot 2^{4}=32\).
questions.hint: The exponent is one less than the index of the requested term.

questions.concept: Determining whether a number is prime
questions.learningObjective: Determine primality by checking for divisors up to the square root of the number.
questions.question: Which statement correctly classifies the integer \(98\) as prime or composite?

options.label: B
options.text: Prime: its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(98\).

questions.explanation: The number has a nontrivial divisor: \(98=2\cdot 49\). Both factors exceed \(1\), so the number is composite.
questions.hint: Try divisors up to the square root; one nontrivial divisor is enough to prove compositeness.

questions.concept: Computing total base-case work across a recursion tree
questions.learningObjective: Combine subproblem count and per-subproblem cost to find total work at the base-case level.
questions.question: A divide-and-conquer algorithm starts with input size \(n=8\). Each non-base call makes \(2\) recursive calls on inputs of half its size. The root is depth \(0\), and all calls reach the base case at depth \(3\), with input size \(1\). Each base-case call performs \(8\) operations. How many operations are performed by all base-case calls combined?
questions.explanation: Each branching level multiplies the number of calls by \(2\). Thus there are \(2^{3}=8\) leaves, and their combined work is \(8\cdot 8=64\) operations.
questions.hint: Count the leaves first, then multiply by the work done at each leaf.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for binary search
questions.learningObjective: Count worst-case key-to-element comparisons in a specified standard binary-search implementation.
questions.question: Standard binary search examines a sorted array of \(n=16\) distinct elements. It uses an inclusive index interval, chooses the lower middle index, and removes the middle element after an unequal comparison. Count one three-way key-to-element comparison per examined element; exclude index and loop-condition checks. What is the maximum number of these comparisons over all present or absent targets?
questions.explanation: The worst remaining interval after one comparison has \(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor\) elements. Hence \(C(0)=0\) and \(C(n)=1+C(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor)\) for \(n\ge 1\). Repeated halving until the interval is empty gives \(C(n)=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\). For this array, \(C(16)=\lfloor\log_2 16\rfloor+1=5\).
questions.hint: Include the comparison with the final remaining element; stopping when only one candidate remains can miss a comparison.

questions.concept: Computing a net workload reduction (delta)
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a net change (delta) between two workload measurements, including its direction.
questions.question: Caching reduces a service's operation count from \(642\) to \(127\) operations per request. By how many operations per request does the count decrease?
questions.explanation: The reduction is the original count minus the new count: \(642-127=515\) operations per request. This positive reduction measures the size of the decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the new count from the original count.

questions.concept: Counting permutations of a set of distinct items
questions.learningObjective: Recall and apply the factorial formula for counting permutations.
questions.question: An algorithm considers every ordering of \(7\) distinct servers. How many orderings are possible?
questions.explanation: There are \(7\) choices for the first position, \(6\) for the next, and so on. The product is \(7!=\prod_{i=1}^{7}i=5040\).
questions.hint: Use the multiplication principle with one fewer available item at each new position.

questions.concept: Applying the Master Theorem to classify a recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Apply the Master Theorem, including the regularity condition when needed, without rounding critical exponents.
questions.question: For \(n=3^k\) with nonnegative integer \(k\), suppose \(T(1)=1\) and \(T(n)=4T\!\left(\frac{n}{3}\right)+n\) for \(n>1\). Which Master Theorem case and tight asymptotic bound apply?
questions.explanation: Here \(a=4\), \(b=3\), and \(f(n)=n\). Because \(4>3^{1}\), \(\log_{3}4>1\). Choose \(\varepsilon=\frac{\log_{3}4-1}{2}>0\); then \(f(n)=O(n^{\log_{3}4-\varepsilon})\). Case \(1\) applies, giving \(T(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_{3}4})\).
questions.hint: Compare the branching factor with the shrink factor raised to the combine-cost exponent; for combine-cost dominance, also check regularity.

questions.concept: Identifying the complexity class of a linear model
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tight asymptotic class of a linear operation-count model.
questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=7n+13\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n}=7+\frac{13}{n}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(7\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.
questions.hint: Identify the highest power with a nonzero positive coefficient.

questions.concept: Solving the characteristic equation of a linear recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Solve a quadratic characteristic equation associated with a linear recurrence relation.
questions.question: A linear recurrence has the characteristic equation \(x^2-x-12=0\). What are its two roots?
questions.explanation:
Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2-x-12&=(x+3)(x-4)\\
(x+3)(x-4)&=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-3\) and \(x=4\). Their sum is \(-3+4=1\) and their product is \((-3)(4)=-12\), matching the coefficients.
questions.hint: Find a pair whose sum is the negative of the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

questions.concept: Inverse proportional scaling of time with number of workers
questions.learningObjective: Solve an inverse-proportion problem relating completion time to the number of parallel workers.
questions.question: A fixed job takes \(21\) minutes with \(6\) identical workers. Assume all work is perfectly divisible, all workers run at the same constant rate, and there is no communication, setup, or sequential overhead. How long does the job take with \(3\) workers?
questions.explanation: The required worker-time is fixed: \(6\cdot 21=126\) worker-minutes. Dividing by the new worker count gives \(\frac{126}{3}=42\) minutes.

questions.concept: Bounding the length of a shortest simple path
questions.learningObjective: Prove and attain the largest possible shortest-path distance in a simple connected unweighted graph.
questions.question: Consider all simple connected undirected unweighted graphs on \(n=7\) vertices and all pairs of distinct vertices in them. What is the largest possible shortest-path length, measured in edges?
questions.explanation: A shortest path cannot repeat a vertex: removing a cycle would shorten it. It therefore visits at most \(7\) vertices and uses at most \(n-1=6\) edges. This bound is achieved by the two endpoints of a path graph on \(7\) vertices, so it is the largest possible value.
questions.hint: Use the no-repeated-vertex bound, then consider the endpoints of a graph that is itself a path.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for linear search
questions.learningObjective: Recall the worst-case comparison count for a linear search over n elements.
questions.question: Linear search checks an unsorted array of \(n=238\) elements one at a time. Count one equality comparison between the target and each examined element. What is the worst-case comparison count when the target may be present or absent?
questions.explanation: If the target is absent, every element must be checked. If it is last, the same number of checks is needed. Thus the maximum is \(n=238\) key-to-element comparisons.
questions.hint: Consider a target that is absent or is the final element checked.

questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n}=5+\frac{19}{n}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(5\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.

questions.concept: Determining whether a number is prime
questions.learningObjective: Determine primality by checking for divisors up to the square root of the number.
questions.question: Which statement correctly classifies the integer \(43\) as prime or composite?

options.label: A
options.text: Composite: it has more than two positive divisors.

options.label: C
options.text: Prime: it has exactly two positive divisors.

questions.explanation: Any composite integer has a factor no larger than its square root. No integer from \(2\) through \(6\) divides \(43\) evenly. Since \(43\) exceeds \(1\), it is prime.
questions.hint: Try divisors up to the square root; one nontrivial divisor is enough to prove compositeness.

questions.concept: Recovering input size from a linear operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Solve a two-step linear equation to recover an algorithm's input size from a measured operation count.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=6n+30\). One run uses \(138\) operations. What is its nonnegative integer input size \(n\)?
questions.explanation:
Undo the fixed cost, then divide by the coefficient:
\[
\begin{aligned}
6n&=138-30=108\\
n&=\frac{108}{6}=18
\end{aligned}
\]
Checking gives \(6\cdot 18+30=138\).
questions.hint: Remove the fixed overhead before dividing by the per-element cost.

questions.concept: Identifying the complexity class of a quadratic model

questions.concept: Expressing a workload change as a signed delta
questions.learningObjective: Correctly interpret a negative signed delta as a decrease, distinct from a negative operation count.
questions.question: A refactor changes a function's operation count from \(77\) to \(7\) operations per call. Define the signed change as \(\Delta=\text{new}-\text{original}\). What is \(\Delta\)?
questions.explanation: Using the specified sign convention, \(\Delta=7-77=-70\) operations per call. The negative sign denotes a decrease; the new operation count itself is \(7\) and remains nonnegative.
questions.hint: Use the stated order of subtraction, and let the sign show the direction of change.

questions.concept: Computing terms of a Fibonacci-style recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Compute terms of a two-term linear recurrence by direct iteration.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers, \(a_0=1\) and \(a_1=3\), while \(a_k=a_{k-1}+a_{k-2}\) for \(k\ge 2\). What is \(a_{6}\)?
questions.explanation:
Build each term from the previous two:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2}&=3+1=4\\
a_{3}&=4+3=7\\
a_{4}&=7+4=11\\
a_{5}&=11+7=18\\
a_{6}&=18+11=29
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(a_{6}=29\).
questions.hint: Start from the two given initial values and compute one new term at a time.

questions.concept: Summing sequential pipeline stage runtimes

questions.explanation: Add the sequential stage durations: \(19+8+13+22+16=78\) milliseconds.

questions.learningObjective: Use the handshake lemma on a realizable simple undirected graph.
questions.question: A simple undirected graph has \(4\) vertices with degree sequence \((2,1,2,1)\). How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: Each edge contributes one degree at each of its two endpoints. The degree sum is \(2+1+2+1=6\), so \(|E|=\frac{6}{2}=3\). The listed sequence has an explicit simple-graph realization, so this degree sum corresponds to a possible graph.
questions.hint: Count how often each edge is included when you add all vertex degrees.

questions.concept: Applying the pigeonhole principle to guarantee a minimum bin size
questions.learningObjective: Apply the pigeonhole principle's ceiling-division bound.
questions.question: \(48\) items are distributed among \(14\) labeled bins. What is the largest integer \(L\) such that every distribution guarantees at least one bin containing \(L\) or more items?
questions.explanation: If every bin held at most \(3\) items, the total would be at most \(14\cdot 3=42\), which is less than \(48\). Therefore some bin has at least \(\left\lceil\frac{48}{14}\right\rceil=4\) items. Distributing the items as evenly as possible attains this largest-bin size, so no stronger guarantee is possible.
questions.hint: Find the ceiling of the average bin size, then check an even distribution to see whether the bound is sharp.

questions.concept: Applying a proportional scale factor to a workload
questions.learningObjective: Apply a proportional scale factor directly to a workload quantity.
questions.question: A model's workload is directly proportional to input size. The current workload is \(16\) operations. If the input size is multiplied by \(2\), what is the new workload?
questions.explanation: Direct proportionality applies the same factor to the workload: \(16\cdot 2=32\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply the original workload by the input-size scale factor.

questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a quadratic time-complexity model with quadratic, linear, and constant terms for a given input size.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=4n^2+3n+18\). How many operations are performed when \(n=10\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute and compute the square first:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(10)&=4\cdot 10^2+3\cdot 10+18\\
&=400+30+18=448
\end{aligned}
\]
The count is \(448\) operations.
questions.hint: Square the input size before multiplying by the leading coefficient.

questions.concept: Counting leaves in a recursion tree
questions.learningObjective: Count the number of base-case invocations in a recursion tree with a fixed branching factor and depth.
questions.question: The root call is at depth \(0\). Every call at a depth less than \(4\) makes exactly \(3\) child calls, and all calls at depth \(4\) are base cases. How many base-case calls are made?
questions.explanation: The number of calls starts at \(1\) and is multiplied by \(3\) at each depth. At depth \(4\), the leaf count is \(3^{4}=81\).
questions.hint: Count one branching multiplication for each edge-depth between the root and a leaf.

questions.concept: Solving a shared-workload equation with algebraic fractions
questions.learningObjective: Clear algebraic fractions to solve for a total workload split across two processes.
questions.question: A workload contains \(n\) items. In one round, two processes handle disjoint parts: the first processes \(\frac{n}{3}\) items and the second processes \(\frac{n}{6}\) items. Together they process \(3\) items in that round; the rest remain for later. What is the total workload \(n\)?
questions.explanation:
Add the two disjoint processed parts:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{n}{3}+\frac{n}{6}&=3\\
9n&=54\\
n&=6
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution gives \(2\) items for the first process and \(1\) for the second, totaling \(3\).
questions.hint: Add the two fractional portions, then clear the denominators.

questions.concept: Identifying the complexity class of a quadratic model
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tight asymptotic class of a quadratic operation-count model.
questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=2n^2+2n+20\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n^2}=2+\frac{2}{n}+\frac{20}{n^2}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(2\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n^2)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.
questions.hint: Identify the highest power with a nonzero positive coefficient.

questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a quadratic time-complexity model with quadratic, linear, and constant terms for a given input size.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=4n^2+3n+12\). How many operations are performed when \(n=7\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute and compute the square first:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(7)&=4\cdot 7^2+3\cdot 7+12\\
&=196+21+12=229
\end{aligned}
\]
The count is \(229\) operations.
questions.hint: Square the input size before multiplying by the leading coefficient.

questions.concept: Counting permutations of a set of distinct items
questions.learningObjective: Recall and apply the factorial formula for counting permutations.
questions.question: An algorithm considers every ordering of \(4\) distinct files. How many orderings are possible?
questions.explanation: There are \(4\) choices for the first position, \(3\) for the next, and so on. The product is \(4!=\prod_{i=1}^{4}i=24\).
questions.hint: Use the multiplication principle with one fewer available item at each new position.

questions.concept: Computing a basic probability as favorable over total outcomes
questions.learningObjective: Apply the basic probability formula: favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
questions.question: A test harness chooses one case uniformly at random from \(14\) cases, of which \(6\) fail. What is the probability of choosing a failing case?
questions.explanation: All cases are equally likely, so \(P(\text{failure})=\frac{6}{14}=\frac{3}{7}\).
questions.hint: Use the number of failing cases divided by the total number of cases.

questions.concept: Solving the characteristic equation of a linear recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Solve a quadratic characteristic equation associated with a linear recurrence relation.
questions.question: A linear recurrence has the characteristic equation \(x^2+2x-24=0\). What are its two roots?
questions.explanation:
Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2+2x-24&=(x+6)(x-4)\\
(x+6)(x-4)&=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-6\) and \(x=4\). Their sum is \(-6+4=-2\) and their product is \((-6)(4)=-24\), matching the coefficients.
questions.hint: Find a pair whose sum is the negative of the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

questions.concept: Interpreting an amortized cost bound
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what an amortized per-operation bound implies about total cost over many operations.
questions.question: Starting from an empty dynamic array, a resizing policy guarantees that the total number of element-copy operations over \(35\) insertions is at most \(5\) times the number of insertions. What is the smallest total upper bound supplied by this guarantee alone?
questions.explanation: Apply the given aggregate guarantee: \(5\cdot 35=175\) element-copy operations. This is an upper bound on the entire sequence; an individual insertion may copy more than \(5\) elements.
questions.hint: Apply the stated bound to the entire insertion sequence, rather than to one worst-case insertion.

questions.concept: Applying the tree edge-count property
questions.learningObjective: Use the edge-count property of a finite tree.
questions.question: A spanning tree connects \(n=14\) vertices of a connected undirected network. How many edges does the tree contain?
questions.explanation: A tree with \(n\) vertices has exactly \(n-1\) edges. Starting with one root, each of the remaining vertices adds one edge to its parent. Here, \(14-1=13\).
questions.hint: In a tree, each vertex other than the root has one edge to its parent.

questions.concept: Expressing a workload change as a signed delta
questions.learningObjective: Correctly interpret a negative signed delta as a decrease, distinct from a negative operation count.
questions.question: A refactor changes a function's operation count from \(52\) to \(21\) operations per call. Define the signed change as \(\Delta=\text{new}-\text{original}\). What is \(\Delta\)?
questions.explanation: Using the specified sign convention, \(\Delta=21-52=-31\) operations per call. The negative sign denotes a decrease; the new operation count itself is \(21\) and remains nonnegative.
questions.hint: Use the stated order of subtraction, and let the sign show the direction of change.

questions.question: Caching reduces a service's operation count from \(330\) to \(295\) operations per request. By how many operations per request does the count decrease?

questions.learningObjective: Determine primality by checking for divisors up to the square root of the number.
questions.question: Which statement correctly classifies the integer \(75\) as prime or composite?

options.label: A
options.text: Prime: its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(75\).

questions.explanation: The number has a nontrivial divisor: \(75=3\cdot 25\). Both factors exceed \(1\), so the number is composite.
questions.hint: Try divisors up to the square root; one nontrivial divisor is enough to prove compositeness.

questions.concept: Computing expected trials until first success (geometric distribution)
questions.learningObjective: Compute the expected number of independent trials up to and including the first success.
questions.question: An algorithm succeeds on each attempt independently with the same probability \(p=\frac{1}{10}\). Let \(X\) count all attempts up to and including the first success. What is \(\mathbb{E}[X]\)?
questions.explanation: One attempt is always made. With probability \(1-p\), a failure leaves the same expected number of additional attempts. Thus \(\mathbb{E}[X]=1+(1-p)\mathbb{E}[X]\), which gives \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{1}{p}=10\). The first successful attempt is included.
questions.hint: After a failed attempt, the remaining task has the same distribution as at the start.

Compare the new count with the original:
\[

\frac{T(3n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{6(3n)^3}{6n^3}\\

\end{aligned}

The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(27\).

questions.question: A batch has a fixed overhead of \(38\) operations and an additional \(4\) operations per item. For a batch of \(5\) items, what is the average number of operations per item? Round the final average to two decimal places when needed.

Add the overhead to the total item cost, then average:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{total}&=38+4\cdot 5=58\\

\end{aligned}
\]
The result is \(11.6\) operations per item. The fixed overhead is spread across the entire batch.

questions.question: \(28\) items are distributed among \(12\) labeled bins. What is the largest integer \(L\) such that every distribution guarantees at least one bin containing \(L\) or more items?
questions.explanation: If every bin held at most \(2\) items, the total would be at most \(12\cdot 2=24\), which is less than \(28\). Therefore some bin has at least \(\left\lceil\frac{28}{12}\right\rceil=3\) items. Distributing the items as evenly as possible attains this largest-bin size, so no stronger guarantee is possible.
questions.hint: Find the ceiling of the average bin size, then check an even distribution to see whether the bound is sharp.

questions.concept: Interpreting an amortized cost bound
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what an amortized per-operation bound implies about total cost over many operations.
questions.question: Starting from an empty dynamic array, a resizing policy guarantees that the total number of element-copy operations over \(50\) insertions is at most \(8\) times the number of insertions. What is the smallest total upper bound supplied by this guarantee alone?
questions.explanation: Apply the given aggregate guarantee: \(8\cdot 50=400\) element-copy operations. This is an upper bound on the entire sequence; an individual insertion may copy more than \(8\) elements.
questions.hint: Apply the stated bound to the entire insertion sequence, rather than to one worst-case insertion.

questions.concept: Interpreting an amortized cost bound
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what an amortized per-operation bound implies about total cost over many operations.
questions.question: Starting from an empty dynamic array, a resizing policy guarantees that the total number of element-copy operations over \(71\) insertions is at most \(8\) times the number of insertions. What is the smallest total upper bound supplied by this guarantee alone?
questions.explanation: Apply the given aggregate guarantee: \(8\cdot 71=568\) element-copy operations. This is an upper bound on the entire sequence; an individual insertion may copy more than \(8\) elements.
questions.hint: Apply the stated bound to the entire insertion sequence, rather than to one worst-case insertion.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=5000\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the smallest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the smallest expression is \(n\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Computing a basic probability as favorable over total outcomes
questions.learningObjective: Apply the basic probability formula: favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
questions.question: A test harness chooses one case uniformly at random from \(44\) cases, of which \(34\) fail. What is the probability of choosing a failing case?
questions.explanation: All cases are equally likely, so \(P(\text{failure})=\frac{34}{44}=\frac{17}{22}\).
questions.hint: Use the number of failing cases divided by the total number of cases.

questions.concept: Applying the tree edge-count property
questions.learningObjective: Use the edge-count property of a finite tree.
questions.question: A spanning tree connects \(n=82\) vertices of a connected undirected network. How many edges does the tree contain?
questions.explanation: A tree with \(n\) vertices has exactly \(n-1\) edges. Starting with one root, each of the remaining vertices adds one edge to its parent. Here, \(82-1=81\).
questions.hint: In a tree, each vertex other than the root has one edge to its parent.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.

questions.concept: Direct proportional scaling of runtime with workload size
questions.learningObjective: Solve a direct-proportion problem relating processing time to workload size.
questions.question: An algorithm processes \(21\) transactions in \(9\) seconds. Its runtime is directly proportional to the number of transactions. How long does it take to process \(7\) transactions at the same rate?
questions.explanation: Time per item remains fixed, so the new time is \(9\cdot\frac{7}{21}=3\) seconds.
questions.hint: Scale the original time by the ratio of the new item count to the original item count.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for linear search
questions.learningObjective: Recall the worst-case comparison count for a linear search over n elements.
questions.question: Linear search checks an unsorted array of \(n=497\) elements one at a time. Count one equality comparison between the target and each examined element. What is the worst-case comparison count when the target may be present or absent?
questions.explanation: If the target is absent, every element must be checked. If it is last, the same number of checks is needed. Thus the maximum is \(n=497\) key-to-element comparisons.
questions.hint: Consider a target that is absent or is the final element checked.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on cubic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a cubic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=5n^3\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(3\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?
questions.explanation:
Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T(3n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{5(3n)^3}{5n^3}\\
&=3^3=27
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(27\).
questions.hint: Substitute the scaled input and form the ratio of the new model to the original.

questions.concept: Counting subproblems at a given recursion level
questions.learningObjective: Determine how many subproblems exist at a given level of a divide-and-conquer recursion tree.
questions.question: A divide-and-conquer algorithm begins with size \(n=8\). Every call with input size greater than \(1\) makes exactly \(3\) calls, each on an input whose size is divided by \(2\). The root is level \(0\). How many calls are at level \(2\)?
questions.explanation: The input size at level \(2\) is \(\frac{8}{2^{2}}=2\), so the tree reaches this level before the base case. Each earlier level multiplies the call count by \(3\), giving \(3^{2}=9\) calls.
questions.hint: Track the branching factor separately from the factor by which input sizes shrink.

questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a quadratic time-complexity model with quadratic, linear, and constant terms for a given input size.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=3n^2+6n+20\). How many operations are performed when \(n=7\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute and compute the square first:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(7)&=3\cdot 7^2+6\cdot 7+20\\
&=147+42+20=209
\end{aligned}
\]
The count is \(209\) operations.
questions.hint: Square the input size before multiplying by the leading coefficient.

questions.concept: Identifying the complexity class of a quadratic model
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tight asymptotic class of a quadratic operation-count model.
questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=4n^2+2n+17\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n^2}=4+\frac{2}{n}+\frac{17}{n^2}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(4\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n^2)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.
questions.hint: Identify the highest power with a nonzero positive coefficient.

questions.concept: Determining whether a number is prime
questions.learningObjective: Determine primality by checking for divisors up to the square root of the number.
questions.question: Which statement correctly classifies the integer \(72\) as prime or composite?

options.label: B
options.text: Prime: its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(72\).

questions.explanation: The number has a nontrivial divisor: \(72=2\cdot 36\). Both factors exceed \(1\), so the number is composite.
questions.hint: Try divisors up to the square root; one nontrivial divisor is enough to prove compositeness.

questions.concept: Applying the Master Theorem to classify a recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Apply the Master Theorem, including the regularity condition when needed, without rounding critical exponents.
questions.question: For \(n=2^k\) with nonnegative integer \(k\), suppose \(T(1)=1\) and \(T(n)=2T\!\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)+1\) for \(n>1\). Which Master Theorem case and tight asymptotic bound apply?
questions.explanation: Here \(a=2\), \(b=2\), and \(f(n)=1\). Because \(2>2^{0}\), \(\log_{2}2>0\). Choose \(\varepsilon=\frac{\log_{2}2-0}{2}>0\); then \(f(n)=O(n^{\log_{2}2-\varepsilon})\). Case \(1\) applies, giving \(T(n)=\Theta(n^{1})\).
questions.hint: Compare the branching factor with the shrink factor raised to the combine-cost exponent; for combine-cost dominance, also check regularity.

questions.concept: Counting combinations (unordered selections)
questions.learningObjective: Count unordered selections without replacement using combinations.
questions.question: A test suite chooses \(6\) distinct test cases from \(7\) available cases without replacement. Order does not matter. How many selections are possible?
questions.explanation: Count ordered choices, then remove the order of the selected group: \(\binom{7}{6}=\frac{7!}{6!(7-6)!}=7\).
questions.hint: Use unordered selections; each selected group has multiple orderings that should be counted only once.

questions.concept: Solving a simple multiplicative recurrence by unrolling

questions.question: A refactor changes a function's operation count from \(187\) to \(34\) operations per call. Define the signed change as \(\Delta=\text{new}-\text{original}\). What is \(\Delta\)?
questions.explanation: Using the specified sign convention, \(\Delta=34-187=-153\) operations per call. The negative sign denotes a decrease; the new operation count itself is \(34\) and remains nonnegative.

questions.concept: Counting steps in the Euclidean algorithm
questions.learningObjective: Trace the Euclidean algorithm to count the number of division steps to compute a GCD.
questions.question: Starting with \((43,12)\), run the Euclidean algorithm to compute \(\gcd(43,12)\). Count every remainder-producing division, including the final division whose remainder is zero. How many division steps are required?
questions.explanation:
The divisions are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
43&=3\cdot 12+7\\
12&=1\cdot 7+5\\
7&=1\cdot 5+2\\
5&=2\cdot 2+1\\
2&=2\cdot 1+0
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(5\) divisions, including the final zero-remainder division. The last nonzero remainder (or divisor at termination) is \(1\), the greatest common divisor.
questions.hint: Record one step for each computed remainder, and include the step that produces zero.

questions.concept: Solving the characteristic equation of a linear recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Solve a quadratic characteristic equation associated with a linear recurrence relation.
questions.question: A linear recurrence has the characteristic equation \(x^2+2x-8=0\). What are its two roots?
questions.explanation:
Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2+2x-8&=(x+4)(x-2)\\
(x+4)(x-2)&=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-4\) and \(x=2\). Their sum is \(-4+2=-2\) and their product is \((-4)(2)=-8\), matching the coefficients.
questions.hint: Find a pair whose sum is the negative of the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

questions.question: A fixed job takes \(36\) minutes with \(7\) identical workers. Assume all work is perfectly divisible, all workers run at the same constant rate, and there is no communication, setup, or sequential overhead. How long does the job take with \(3\) workers?
questions.explanation: The required worker-time is fixed: \(7\cdot 36=252\) worker-minutes. Dividing by the new worker count gives \(\frac{252}{3}=84\) minutes.

questions.concept: Computing terms of a Fibonacci-style recurrence

questions.question: For nonnegative integers, \(a_0=5\) and \(a_1=4\), while \(a_k=a_{k-1}+a_{k-2}\) for \(k\ge 2\). What is \(a_{6}\)?
questions.explanation:
Build each term from the previous two:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2}&=4+5=9\\
a_{3}&=9+4=13\\
a_{4}&=13+9=22\\
a_{5}&=22+13=35\\
a_{6}&=35+22=57
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(a_{6}=57\).
questions.hint: Start from the two given initial values and compute one new term at a time.

questions.concept: Distinguishing recursive and iterative algorithm structures

questions.question: A function repeatedly calls itself without reaching a stopping condition. Each call retains a stack frame while waiting for the next call; the runtime has finite stack memory and no tail-call optimization. What can happen?

options.label: A
options.text: The runtime must automatically convert the calls into an iterative loop.

options.label: B
options.text: The pending calls can exhaust the stack memory.

options.label: C
options.text: The runtime must skip every second call to conserve memory.

questions.explanation: Every pending call retains a frame. Since no stopping condition is reached, the frame count grows without bound and eventually exceeds finite stack memory, causing stack exhaustion. The runtime does not automatically replace the calls with a loop or skip alternating calls.
questions.hint: Consider the memory retained by calls that have not yet returned.

\end{aligned}

questions.concept: Counting steps in the Euclidean algorithm
questions.learningObjective: Trace the Euclidean algorithm to count the number of division steps to compute a GCD.
questions.question: Starting with \((108,77)\), run the Euclidean algorithm to compute \(\gcd(108,77)\). Count every remainder-producing division, including the final division whose remainder is zero. How many division steps are required?
questions.explanation:
The divisions are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
108&=1\cdot 77+31\\
77&=2\cdot 31+15\\
31&=2\cdot 15+1\\
15&=15\cdot 1+0
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(4\) divisions, including the final zero-remainder division. The last nonzero remainder (or divisor at termination) is \(1\), the greatest common divisor.
questions.hint: Record one step for each computed remainder, and include the step that produces zero.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=50001\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the smallest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the smallest expression is \(n\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Solving the characteristic equation of a linear recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Solve a quadratic characteristic equation associated with a linear recurrence relation.
questions.question: A linear recurrence has the characteristic equation \(x^2-16=0\). What are its two roots?
questions.explanation:
Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2-16&=(x+4)(x-4)\\
(x+4)(x-4)&=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-4\) and \(x=4\). Their sum is \(-4+4=0\) and their product is \((-4)(4)=-16\), matching the coefficients.
questions.hint: Find a pair whose sum is the negative of the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

questions.concept: Solving the characteristic equation of a linear recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Solve a quadratic characteristic equation associated with a linear recurrence relation.
questions.question: A linear recurrence has the characteristic equation \(x^2+3x-28=0\). What are its two roots?
questions.explanation:
Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2+3x-28&=(x+7)(x-4)\\
(x+7)(x-4)&=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-7\) and \(x=4\). Their sum is \(-7+4=-3\) and their product is \((-7)(4)=-28\), matching the coefficients.
questions.hint: Find a pair whose sum is the negative of the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

questions.concept: Expressing a workload change as a signed delta
questions.learningObjective: Correctly interpret a negative signed delta as a decrease, distinct from a negative operation count.
questions.question: A refactor changes a function's operation count from \(158\) to \(124\) operations per call. Define the signed change as \(\Delta=\text{new}-\text{original}\). What is \(\Delta\)?
questions.explanation: Using the specified sign convention, \(\Delta=124-158=-34\) operations per call. The negative sign denotes a decrease; the new operation count itself is \(124\) and remains nonnegative.
questions.hint: Use the stated order of subtraction, and let the sign show the direction of change.

questions.concept: Computing amortized per-item cost for a batch operation
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish per-item cost from amortized cost, which spreads the fixed overhead across the whole batch.
questions.question: A batch has a fixed overhead of \(21\) operations and an additional \(8\) operations per item. For a batch of \(36\) items, what is the average number of operations per item? Round the final average to two decimal places when needed.
questions.explanation:
Add the overhead to the total item cost, then average:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{total}&=21+8\cdot 36=309\\
\text{average}&=\frac{309}{36}\approx 8.58
\end{aligned}
\]
The result is \(8.58\) operations per item. The fixed overhead is spread across the entire batch.
questions.hint: First find the total batch cost, including overhead; then divide by the number of items.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for binary search
questions.learningObjective: Count worst-case key-to-element comparisons in a specified standard binary-search implementation.
questions.question: Standard binary search examines a sorted array of \(n=128\) distinct elements. It uses an inclusive index interval, chooses the lower middle index, and removes the middle element after an unequal comparison. Count one three-way key-to-element comparison per examined element; exclude index and loop-condition checks. What is the maximum number of these comparisons over all present or absent targets?
questions.explanation: The worst remaining interval after one comparison has \(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor\) elements. Hence \(C(0)=0\) and \(C(n)=1+C(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor)\) for \(n\ge 1\). Repeated halving until the interval is empty gives \(C(n)=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\). For this array, \(C(128)=\lfloor\log_2 128\rfloor+1=8\).
questions.hint: Include the comparison with the final remaining element; stopping when only one candidate remains can miss a comparison.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes (largest case)

questions.concept: Computing expected trials until first success (geometric distribution)
questions.learningObjective: Compute the expected number of independent trials up to and including the first success.
questions.question: An algorithm succeeds on each attempt independently with the same probability \(p=\frac{1}{18}\). Let \(X\) count all attempts up to and including the first success. What is \(\mathbb{E}[X]\)?
questions.explanation: One attempt is always made. With probability \(1-p\), a failure leaves the same expected number of additional attempts. Thus \(\mathbb{E}[X]=1+(1-p)\mathbb{E}[X]\), which gives \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{1}{p}=18\). The first successful attempt is included.
questions.hint: After a failed attempt, the remaining task has the same distribution as at the start.

questions.concept: Expressing a workload change as a signed delta

questions.concept: Applying the tree edge-count property
questions.learningObjective: Use the edge-count property of a finite tree.
questions.question: A spanning tree connects \(n=81\) vertices of a connected undirected network. How many edges does the tree contain?
questions.explanation: A tree with \(n\) vertices has exactly \(n-1\) edges. Starting with one root, each of the remaining vertices adds one edge to its parent. Here, \(81-1=80\).
questions.hint: In a tree, each vertex other than the root has one edge to its parent.

questions.concept: Computing throughput from total items and elapsed time
questions.learningObjective: Compute throughput as items processed divided by elapsed time.
questions.question: A pipeline processes \(792\) records in \(18\) seconds at a steady rate. What is its throughput in records per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput is the number of processed items divided by elapsed time: \(\frac{792}{18}=44\) records per second.
questions.hint: Divide the total number of processed items by the elapsed time.

questions.concept: Computing terms of a Fibonacci-style recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Compute terms of a two-term linear recurrence by direct iteration.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers, \(a_0=5\) and \(a_1=4\), while \(a_k=a_{k-1}+a_{k-2}\) for \(k\ge 2\). What is \(a_{4}\)?
questions.explanation:
Build each term from the previous two:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2}&=4+5=9\\
a_{3}&=9+4=13\\
a_{4}&=13+9=22
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(a_{4}=22\).
questions.hint: Start from the two given initial values and compute one new term at a time.

questions.concept: Applying the Master Theorem to classify a recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Apply the Master Theorem, including the regularity condition when needed, without rounding critical exponents.
questions.question: For \(n=3^k\) with nonnegative integer \(k\), suppose \(T(1)=1\) and \(T(n)=3T\!\left(\frac{n}{3}\right)+n\) for \(n>1\). Which Master Theorem case and tight asymptotic bound apply?
questions.explanation: Because \(3=3^{1}\), the critical exponent is \(\log_{3}3=1\). The combine cost matches \(n^{\log_{3}3}\), so Case \(2\) gives \(T(n)=\Theta(n\log n)\).
questions.hint: Compare the branching factor with the shrink factor raised to the combine-cost exponent; for combine-cost dominance, also check regularity.

questions.concept: Computing a term of a geometric sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute a requested term from the first term and common ratio of a geometric sequence.
questions.question: A geometric sequence has \(a_1=6\) and common ratio \(2\). What is \(a_{6}\)?
questions.explanation: The first term is multiplied by the common ratio \(5\) times to reach term \(6\): \(a_{6}=6\cdot 2^{5}=192\).
questions.hint: The exponent is one less than the index of the requested term.

questions.concept: Determining whether a number is prime
questions.learningObjective: Determine primality by checking for divisors up to the square root of the number.
questions.question: Which statement correctly classifies the integer \(74\) as prime or composite?

options.label: B
options.text: Prime: its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(74\).

questions.explanation: The number has a nontrivial divisor: \(74=2\cdot 37\). Both factors exceed \(1\), so the number is composite.
questions.hint: Try divisors up to the square root; one nontrivial divisor is enough to prove compositeness.

questions.concept: Computing a term of a geometric sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute a requested term from the first term and common ratio of a geometric sequence.
questions.question: A geometric sequence has \(a_1=6\) and common ratio \(2\). What is \(a_{5}\)?

questions.concept: Counting permutations of a set of distinct items
questions.learningObjective: Recall and apply the factorial formula for counting permutations.
questions.question: An algorithm considers every ordering of \(8\) distinct tasks. How many orderings are possible?
questions.explanation: There are \(8\) choices for the first position, \(7\) for the next, and so on. The product is \(8!=\prod_{i=1}^{8}i=40320\).
questions.hint: Use the multiplication principle with one fewer available item at each new position.

questions.concept: Counting subproblems at a given recursion level
questions.learningObjective: Determine how many subproblems exist at a given level of a divide-and-conquer recursion tree.
questions.question: A divide-and-conquer algorithm begins with size \(n=32\). Every call with input size greater than \(1\) makes exactly \(4\) calls, each on an input whose size is divided by \(2\). The root is level \(0\). How many calls are at level \(4\)?
questions.explanation: The input size at level \(4\) is \(\frac{32}{2^{4}}=2\), so the tree reaches this level before the base case. Each earlier level multiplies the call count by \(4\), giving \(4^{4}=256\) calls.
questions.hint: Track the branching factor separately from the factor by which input sizes shrink.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for linear search
questions.learningObjective: Recall the worst-case comparison count for a linear search over n elements.
questions.question: Linear search checks an unsorted array of \(n=453\) elements one at a time. Count one equality comparison between the target and each examined element. What is the worst-case comparison count when the target may be present or absent?
questions.explanation: If the target is absent, every element must be checked. If it is last, the same number of checks is needed. Thus the maximum is \(n=453\) key-to-element comparisons.
questions.hint: Consider a target that is absent or is the final element checked.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for linear search
questions.learningObjective: Recall the worst-case comparison count for a linear search over n elements.
questions.question: Linear search checks an unsorted array of \(n=69\) elements one at a time. Count one equality comparison between the target and each examined element. What is the worst-case comparison count when the target may be present or absent?
