questions.concept: Direct proportional scaling of runtime with workload size
questions.learningObjective: Solve a direct-proportion problem relating processing time to workload size.
questions.question: An algorithm processes \(23\) rows in \(19\) time-units. Its runtime is directly proportional to the number of rows. How long does it take to process \(22\) rows at the same rate?
questions.explanation: Time per item remains fixed, so the new time is \(19\cdot\frac{22}{23}=\frac{418}{23}\) time-units.
questions.hint: Scale the original time by the ratio of the new item count to the original item count.

questions.concept: Computing a net workload reduction (delta)
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a net change (delta) between two workload measurements, including its direction.
questions.question: Caching reduces a service's operation count from \(879\) to \(616\) operations per request. By how many operations per request does the count decrease?
questions.explanation: The reduction is the original count minus the new count: \(879-616=263\) operations per request. This positive reduction measures the size of the decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the new count from the original count.

questions.concept: Computing a basic probability as favorable over total outcomes
questions.learningObjective: Apply the basic probability formula: favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
questions.question: A test harness chooses one case uniformly at random from \(31\) cases, of which \(1\) fail. What is the probability of choosing a failing case?
questions.explanation: All cases are equally likely, so \(P(\text{failure})=\frac{1}{31}=\frac{1}{31}\).
questions.hint: Use the number of failing cases divided by the total number of cases.

questions.concept: Applying the pigeonhole principle to guarantee a minimum bin size
questions.learningObjective: Apply the pigeonhole principle's ceiling-division bound.
questions.question: \(26\) items are distributed among \(7\) labeled bins. What is the largest integer \(L\) such that every distribution guarantees at least one bin containing \(L\) or more items?
questions.explanation: If every bin held at most \(3\) items, the total would be at most \(7\cdot 3=21\), which is less than \(26\). Therefore some bin has at least \(\left\lceil\frac{26}{7}\right\rceil=4\) items. Distributing the items as evenly as possible attains this largest-bin size, so no stronger guarantee is possible.
questions.hint: Find the ceiling of the average bin size, then check an even distribution to see whether the bound is sharp.

The result is \(10.15\) operations per item. The fixed overhead is spread across the entire batch.

questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a quadratic time-complexity model with quadratic, linear, and constant terms for a given input size.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=n^2+4n+1\). How many operations are performed when \(n=3\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute and compute the square first:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(3)&=1\cdot 3^2+4\cdot 3+1\\
&=9+12+1=22
\end{aligned}
\]
The count is \(22\) operations.

options.label: A

options.label: C
options.text: Prime: it has exactly two positive divisors.

questions.explanation: Any composite integer has a factor no larger than its square root. No integer from \(2\) through \(4\) divides \(23\) evenly. Since \(23\) exceeds \(1\), it is prime.

questions.explanation: There are \(6\) steps from the base case, and each adds \(3\). Therefore, \(T(6)=2+6\cdot 3=20\).

questions.explanation: Each edge joins one unordered pair of distinct vertices. Therefore, \(\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\). Substituting \(n=9\) gives \(\frac{9\cdot 8}{2}=36\).

questions.concept: Distinguishing recursive and iterative algorithm structures
questions.learningObjective: Understand the structural requirements and behavior of recursion versus iteration.
questions.question: A recursive procedure is intended to terminate for every nonnegative integer input. Each call performs finite nonrecursive work and makes finitely many recursive calls. Which design supplies a termination argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a base case at zero and a nonnegative integer measure that strictly decreases on every recursive call.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a counter that increases on every recursive call, regardless of the stopping condition.

options.label: C
options.text: Store the input in a global variable, regardless of whether recursive calls make progress.

questions.explanation: A nonnegative integer measure cannot decrease strictly forever. If each recursive call reduces that measure and the procedure stops when it reaches zero, each branch has finite depth. Together with the stated finite work and finite branching, this makes the whole computation finite. A global counter or variable alone does not establish progress toward a stopping condition.
questions.hint: Identify both a stopping condition and a measure that moves strictly toward it.

questions.concept: Bounding the length of a shortest simple path

questions.explanation: A shortest path cannot repeat a vertex: removing a cycle would shorten it. It therefore visits at most \(12\) vertices and uses at most \(n-1=11\) edges. This bound is achieved by the two endpoints of a path graph on \(12\) vertices, so it is the largest possible value.
questions.hint: Use the no-repeated-vertex bound, then consider the endpoints of a graph that is itself a path.

questions.concept: Recovering input size from a linear operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Solve a two-step linear equation to recover an algorithm's input size from a measured operation count.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=5n+11\). One run uses \(106\) operations. What is its nonnegative integer input size \(n\)?
questions.explanation:
Undo the fixed cost, then divide by the coefficient:
\[
\begin{aligned}
5n&=106-11=95\\
n&=\frac{95}{5}=19
\end{aligned}
\]
Checking gives \(5\cdot 19+11=106\).
questions.hint: Remove the fixed overhead before dividing by the per-element cost.

questions.concept: Identifying the complexity class of a linear model
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tight asymptotic class of a linear operation-count model.
questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=3n+12\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n}=3+\frac{12}{n}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(3\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.
questions.hint: Identify the highest power with a nonzero positive coefficient.

questions.concept: Computing amortized per-item cost for a batch operation
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish per-item cost from amortized cost, which spreads the fixed overhead across the whole batch.
questions.question: A batch has a fixed overhead of \(60\) operations and an additional \(6\) operations per item. For a batch of \(47\) items, what is the average number of operations per item? Round the final average to two decimal places when needed.
questions.explanation:
Add the overhead to the total item cost, then average:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{total}&=60+6\cdot 47=342\\
\text{average}&=\frac{342}{47}\approx 7.28
\end{aligned}
\]
The result is \(7.28\) operations per item. The fixed overhead is spread across the entire batch.
questions.hint: First find the total batch cost, including overhead; then divide by the number of items.

questions.concept: Direct proportional scaling of runtime with workload size
questions.learningObjective: Solve a direct-proportion problem relating processing time to workload size.
questions.question: An algorithm processes \(6\) documents in \(13\) milliseconds. Its runtime is directly proportional to the number of documents. How long does it take to process \(26\) documents at the same rate?
questions.explanation: Time per item remains fixed, so the new time is \(13\cdot\frac{26}{6}=\frac{169}{3}\) milliseconds.
questions.hint: Scale the original time by the ratio of the new item count to the original item count.

questions.concept: Computing a term of a geometric sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute a requested term from the first term and common ratio of a geometric sequence.
questions.question: A geometric sequence has \(a_1=3\) and common ratio \(3\). What is \(a_{5}\)?
questions.explanation: The first term is multiplied by the common ratio \(4\) times to reach term \(5\): \(a_{5}=3\cdot 3^{4}=243\).
questions.hint: The exponent is one less than the index of the requested term.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for linear search
questions.learningObjective: Recall the worst-case comparison count for a linear search over n elements.
questions.question: Linear search checks an unsorted array of \(n=84\) elements one at a time. Count one equality comparison between the target and each examined element. What is the worst-case comparison count when the target may be present or absent?
questions.explanation: If the target is absent, every element must be checked. If it is last, the same number of checks is needed. Thus the maximum is \(n=84\) key-to-element comparisons.
questions.hint: Consider a target that is absent or is the final element checked.

questions.concept: Solving the characteristic equation of a linear recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Solve a quadratic characteristic equation associated with a linear recurrence relation.
questions.question: A linear recurrence has the characteristic equation \(x^2+x-20=0\). What are its two roots?
questions.explanation:
Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2+x-20&=(x+5)(x-4)\\
(x+5)(x-4)&=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-5\) and \(x=4\). Their sum is \(-5+4=-1\) and their product is \((-5)(4)=-20\), matching the coefficients.
questions.hint: Find a pair whose sum is the negative of the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

questions.concept: Computing throughput from total items and elapsed time
questions.learningObjective: Compute throughput as items processed divided by elapsed time.
questions.question: A pipeline processes \(504\) records in \(21\) seconds at a steady rate. What is its throughput in records per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput is the number of processed items divided by elapsed time: \(\frac{504}{21}=24\) records per second.
questions.hint: Divide the total number of processed items by the elapsed time.

questions.concept: Computing a value modulo m for hash bucket assignment
questions.learningObjective: Apply the modulo operation to compute a hash bucket index.
questions.question: A hash table assigns key \(254\) to bucket \(254\bmod 20\). What is the bucket index, using remainders from \(0\) through \(19\)?
questions.explanation: Euclidean division gives \(254=20\cdot 12+14\). Since \(0\le 14<20\), the remainder and bucket index are \(14\).

questions.concept: Applying the Master Theorem to classify a recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Apply the Master Theorem, including the regularity condition when needed, without rounding critical exponents.
questions.question: For \(n=3^k\) with nonnegative integer \(k\), suppose \(T(1)=1\) and \(T(n)=3T\!\left(\frac{n}{3}\right)+1\) for \(n>1\). Which Master Theorem case and tight asymptotic bound apply?
questions.explanation: Here \(a=3\), \(b=3\), and \(f(n)=1\). Because \(3>3^{0}\), \(\log_{3}3>0\). Choose \(\varepsilon=\frac{\log_{3}3-0}{2}>0\); then \(f(n)=O(n^{\log_{3}3-\varepsilon})\). Case \(1\) applies, giving \(T(n)=\Theta(n^{1})\).
questions.hint: Compare the branching factor with the shrink factor raised to the combine-cost exponent; for combine-cost dominance, also check regularity.

questions.concept: Computing a basic probability as favorable over total outcomes
questions.learningObjective: Apply the basic probability formula: favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
questions.question: A test harness chooses one case uniformly at random from \(14\) cases, of which \(9\) fail. What is the probability of choosing a failing case?
questions.explanation: All cases are equally likely, so \(P(\text{failure})=\frac{9}{14}=\frac{9}{14}\).
questions.hint: Use the number of failing cases divided by the total number of cases.

questions.concept: Computing total base-case work across a recursion tree
questions.learningObjective: Combine subproblem count and per-subproblem cost to find total work at the base-case level.
questions.question: A divide-and-conquer algorithm starts with input size \(n=32\). Each non-base call makes \(2\) recursive calls on inputs of half its size. The root is depth \(0\), and all calls reach the base case at depth \(5\), with input size \(1\). Each base-case call performs \(8\) operations. How many operations are performed by all base-case calls combined?
questions.explanation: Each branching level multiplies the number of calls by \(2\). Thus there are \(2^{5}=32\) leaves, and their combined work is \(32\cdot 8=256\) operations.
questions.hint: Count the leaves first, then multiply by the work done at each leaf.

questions.concept: Computing a runtime after a percentage reduction
questions.learningObjective: Apply a percentage decrease to a runtime value.
questions.question: An optimization reduces a routine's runtime of \(316\) milliseconds by \(40\%\). What is the exact new runtime?
questions.explanation:
Apply the percentage exactly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{reduction}&=316\cdot\frac{40}{100}=126.4\\
\text{new runtime}&=316-126.4=189.6
\end{aligned}
\]
The new runtime is \(189.6\) milliseconds; no integer rounding is applied.
questions.hint: Multiply the original runtime by the fraction that remains after the reduction.

questions.concept: Counting edges in a complete graph
questions.learningObjective: Count the unordered vertex pairs of a simple undirected complete graph.
questions.question: How many edges are in a simple undirected complete graph with \(n=6\) vertices?
questions.explanation: Each edge joins one unordered pair of distinct vertices. Therefore, \(\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\). Substituting \(n=6\) gives \(\frac{6\cdot 5}{2}=15\).
questions.hint: Count unordered pairs of distinct vertices.

questions.concept: Bounding the length of a shortest simple path

questions.question: Consider all simple connected undirected unweighted graphs on \(n=13\) vertices and all pairs of distinct vertices in them. What is the largest possible shortest-path length, measured in edges?
questions.explanation: A shortest path cannot repeat a vertex: removing a cycle would shorten it. It therefore visits at most \(13\) vertices and uses at most \(n-1=12\) edges. This bound is achieved by the two endpoints of a path graph on \(13\) vertices, so it is the largest possible value.

\[
\begin{aligned}
8n+2&=3n+42\\
5n&=40\\
n&=8
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution gives \(8(8)+2=66\) for A and \(3(8)+42=66\) for B.
questions.hint: Equate the two expressions and collect the terms containing the input size.

Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T(3n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{10(3n)^2}{10n^2}\\
&=3^2=9
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(9\).
questions.hint: Substitute the scaled input and form the ratio of the new model to the original.

Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:

x^2-5x-6&=(x+1)(x-6)\\

\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-1\) and \(x=6\). Their sum is \(-1+6=5\) and their product is \((-1)(6)=-6\), matching the coefficients.

questions.explanation:
Add the overhead to the total item cost, then average:
\[
\begin{aligned}

\]
The result is \(8.2\) operations per item. The fixed overhead is spread across the entire batch.

questions.concept: Applying the pigeonhole principle to guarantee a minimum bin size
questions.learningObjective: Apply the pigeonhole principle's ceiling-division bound.
questions.question: \(27\) items are distributed among \(8\) labeled bins. What is the largest integer \(L\) such that every distribution guarantees at least one bin containing \(L\) or more items?
questions.explanation: If every bin held at most \(3\) items, the total would be at most \(8\cdot 3=24\), which is less than \(27\). Therefore some bin has at least \(\left\lceil\frac{27}{8}\right\rceil=4\) items. Distributing the items as evenly as possible attains this largest-bin size, so no stronger guarantee is possible.
questions.hint: Find the ceiling of the average bin size, then check an even distribution to see whether the bound is sharp.

questions.hint: Equate the two expressions and collect the terms containing the input size.

questions.concept: Solving a simple additive recurrence by unrolling
questions.learningObjective: Solve a linear recurrence with a fixed additive increment by unrolling it to the base case.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers \(n\), a recurrence satisfies \(T(n)=T(n-1)+4\) for \(n\ge 1\), with \(T(0)=7\). What is \(T(4)\)?
questions.explanation: There are \(4\) steps from the base case, and each adds \(4\). Therefore, \(T(4)=7+4\cdot 4=23\).
questions.hint: Count the steps from the base case and add the increment once per step.

questions.concept: Solving the characteristic equation of a linear recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Solve a quadratic characteristic equation associated with a linear recurrence relation.
questions.question: A linear recurrence has the characteristic equation \(x^2+3x-4=0\). What are its two roots?
questions.explanation:
Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2+3x-4&=(x+4)(x-1)\\
(x+4)(x-1)&=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-4\) and \(x=1\). Their sum is \(-4+1=-3\) and their product is \((-4)(1)=-4\), matching the coefficients.
questions.hint: Find a pair whose sum is the negative of the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=1001\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the smallest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the smallest expression is \(n\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on quadratic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a quadratic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=11n^2\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(3\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?
questions.explanation:
Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T(3n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{11(3n)^2}{11n^2}\\
&=3^2=9
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(9\).
questions.hint: Substitute the scaled input and form the ratio of the new model to the original.

questions.concept: Expressing a workload change as a signed delta
questions.learningObjective: Correctly interpret a negative signed delta as a decrease, distinct from a negative operation count.
questions.question: A refactor changes a function's operation count from \(136\) to \(25\) operations per call. Define the signed change as \(\Delta=\text{new}-\text{original}\). What is \(\Delta\)?
questions.explanation: Using the specified sign convention, \(\Delta=25-136=-111\) operations per call. The negative sign denotes a decrease; the new operation count itself is \(25\) and remains nonnegative.
questions.hint: Use the stated order of subtraction, and let the sign show the direction of change.

questions.concept: Counting permutations of a set of distinct items
questions.learningObjective: Recall and apply the factorial formula for counting permutations.
questions.question: An algorithm considers every ordering of \(13\) distinct jobs. How many orderings are possible?
questions.explanation: There are \(13\) choices for the first position, \(12\) for the next, and so on. The product is \(13!=\prod_{i=1}^{13}i=6227020800\).
questions.hint: Use the multiplication principle with one fewer available item at each new position.

questions.concept: Applying a proportional scale factor to a workload
questions.learningObjective: Apply a proportional scale factor directly to a workload quantity.
questions.question: A model's workload is directly proportional to input size. The current workload is \(28\) operations. If the input size is multiplied by \(6\), what is the new workload?
questions.explanation: Direct proportionality applies the same factor to the workload: \(28\cdot 6=168\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply the original workload by the input-size scale factor.

questions.concept: Counting steps in the Euclidean algorithm
questions.learningObjective: Trace the Euclidean algorithm to count the number of division steps to compute a GCD.
questions.question: Starting with \((27,8)\), run the Euclidean algorithm to compute \(\gcd(27,8)\). Count every remainder-producing division, including the final division whose remainder is zero. How many division steps are required?
questions.explanation:
The divisions are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
27&=3\cdot 8+3\\
8&=2\cdot 3+2\\
3&=1\cdot 2+1\\
2&=2\cdot 1+0
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(4\) divisions, including the final zero-remainder division. The last nonzero remainder (or divisor at termination) is \(1\), the greatest common divisor.
questions.hint: Record one step for each computed remainder, and include the step that produces zero.

questions.concept: Computing a basic probability as favorable over total outcomes
questions.learningObjective: Apply the basic probability formula: favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
questions.question: A test harness chooses one case uniformly at random from \(17\) cases, of which \(9\) fail. What is the probability of choosing a failing case?
questions.explanation: All cases are equally likely, so \(P(\text{failure})=\frac{9}{17}=\frac{9}{17}\).
questions.hint: Use the number of failing cases divided by the total number of cases.

questions.concept: Counting edges in a complete graph
questions.learningObjective: Count the unordered vertex pairs of a simple undirected complete graph.
questions.question: How many edges are in a simple undirected complete graph with \(n=14\) vertices?
questions.explanation: Each edge joins one unordered pair of distinct vertices. Therefore, \(\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\). Substituting \(n=14\) gives \(\frac{14\cdot 13}{2}=91\).
questions.hint: Count unordered pairs of distinct vertices.

questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a quadratic time-complexity model with quadratic, linear, and constant terms for a given input size.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=4n^2+n+3\). How many operations are performed when \(n=7\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute and compute the square first:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(7)&=4\cdot 7^2+1\cdot 7+3\\
&=196+7+3=206
\end{aligned}
\]
The count is \(206\) operations.
questions.hint: Square the input size before multiplying by the leading coefficient.

questions.concept: Summing sequential pipeline stage runtimes
questions.learningObjective: Sum the runtimes of sequential pipeline stages to find total processing time.
questions.question: One item passes through \(3\) sequential pipeline stages taking \(21\), \(5\), \(7\) milliseconds, respectively. The item incurs no other delay, and its stages do not overlap. What is its total processing time?
questions.explanation: Add the sequential stage durations: \(21+5+7=33\) milliseconds.
questions.hint: The same item completes each stage before starting the next.

questions.concept: Counting combinations (unordered selections)
questions.learningObjective: Count unordered selections without replacement using combinations.
questions.question: A test suite chooses \(11\) distinct test cases from \(15\) available cases without replacement. Order does not matter. How many selections are possible?
questions.explanation: Count ordered choices, then remove the order of the selected group: \(\binom{15}{11}=\frac{15!}{11!(15-11)!}=1365\).
questions.hint: Use unordered selections; each selected group has multiple orderings that should be counted only once.

questions.concept: Computing geometric growth over repeated rounds
questions.learningObjective: Apply the geometric growth repeated-multiplication model.
questions.question: A crawler starts with \(23\) discovered pages at round \(0\). Its discovered-page count is multiplied by \(3\) at the end of every round. How many pages are counted after \(6\) rounds?
questions.explanation: The growth factor is applied once per round: \(23\cdot 3^{6}=23\cdot 729=16767\) pages.
questions.hint: Use one multiplication by the growth factor for each completed round.

questions.explanation: Substitute the input size: \(T(9)=5\cdot 9+28=73\) operations.

questions.concept: Applying the pigeonhole principle to guarantee a minimum bin size
questions.learningObjective: Apply the pigeonhole principle's ceiling-division bound.
questions.question: \(12\) items are distributed among \(5\) labeled bins. What is the largest integer \(L\) such that every distribution guarantees at least one bin containing \(L\) or more items?
questions.explanation: If every bin held at most \(2\) items, the total would be at most \(5\cdot 2=10\), which is less than \(12\). Therefore some bin has at least \(\left\lceil\frac{12}{5}\right\rceil=3\) items. Distributing the items as evenly as possible attains this largest-bin size, so no stronger guarantee is possible.
questions.hint: Find the ceiling of the average bin size, then check an even distribution to see whether the bound is sharp.

questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=n^2+9n+20\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n^2}=1+\frac{9}{n}+\frac{20}{n^2}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(1\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n^2)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.
questions.hint: Identify the highest power with a nonzero positive coefficient.

questions.concept: Computing a runtime after a percentage reduction
questions.learningObjective: Apply a percentage decrease to a runtime value.
questions.question: An optimization reduces a routine's runtime of \(362\) milliseconds by \(10\%\). What is the exact new runtime?
questions.explanation:
Apply the percentage exactly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{reduction}&=362\cdot\frac{10}{100}=36.2\\
\text{new runtime}&=362-36.2=325.8
\end{aligned}
\]
The new runtime is \(325.8\) milliseconds; no integer rounding is applied.
questions.hint: Multiply the original runtime by the fraction that remains after the reduction.

questions.learningObjective: Use the handshake lemma on a realizable simple undirected graph.
questions.question: A simple undirected graph has \(8\) vertices with degree sequence \((7,2,5,2,1,4,4,5)\). How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: Each edge contributes one degree at each of its two endpoints. The degree sum is \(7+2+5+2+1+4+4+5=30\), so \(|E|=\frac{30}{2}=15\). The listed sequence has an explicit simple-graph realization, so this degree sum corresponds to a possible graph.
questions.hint: Count how often each edge is included when you add all vertex degrees.

questions.concept: Direct proportional scaling of runtime with workload size
questions.learningObjective: Solve a direct-proportion problem relating processing time to workload size.

questions.concept: Solving a simple multiplicative recurrence by unrolling
questions.learningObjective: Solve a linear recurrence with a fixed multiplicative factor by unrolling it to the base case.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers \(n\), \(T(0)=3\) and \(T(n)=3T(n-1)\) for \(n\ge 1\). What is \(T(5)\)?
questions.explanation: Apply the multiplier \(3\) once for each of \(5\) steps: \(T(5)=3\cdot 3^{5}=729\).
questions.hint: Start with the base value and count one multiplication per recurrence step.

questions.concept: Computing a term of a geometric sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute a requested term from the first term and common ratio of a geometric sequence.
questions.question: A geometric sequence has \(a_1=3\) and common ratio \(4\). What is \(a_{4}\)?
questions.explanation: The first term is multiplied by the common ratio \(3\) times to reach term \(4\): \(a_{4}=3\cdot 4^{3}=192\).
questions.hint: The exponent is one less than the index of the requested term.

questions.concept: Expressing a workload change as a signed delta
questions.learningObjective: Correctly interpret a negative signed delta as a decrease, distinct from a negative operation count.
questions.question: A refactor changes a function's operation count from \(128\) to \(88\) operations per call. Define the signed change as \(\Delta=\text{new}-\text{original}\). What is \(\Delta\)?
questions.explanation: Using the specified sign convention, \(\Delta=88-128=-40\) operations per call. The negative sign denotes a decrease; the new operation count itself is \(88\) and remains nonnegative.
questions.hint: Use the stated order of subtraction, and let the sign show the direction of change.

questions.concept: Identifying the complexity class of a linear model
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tight asymptotic class of a linear operation-count model.
questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=7n+9\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n}=7+\frac{9}{n}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(7\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.
questions.hint: Identify the highest power with a nonzero positive coefficient.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on quadratic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a quadratic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=11n^2\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(4\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?
questions.explanation:
Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T(4n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{11(4n)^2}{11n^2}\\
&=4^2=16
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(16\).
questions.hint: Substitute the scaled input and form the ratio of the new model to the original.

questions.concept: Solving the characteristic equation of a linear recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Solve a quadratic characteristic equation associated with a linear recurrence relation.
questions.question: A linear recurrence has the characteristic equation \(x^2+4x-5=0\). What are its two roots?
questions.explanation:
Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2+4x-5&=(x+5)(x-1)\\
(x+5)(x-1)&=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-5\) and \(x=1\). Their sum is \(-5+1=-4\) and their product is \((-5)(1)=-5\), matching the coefficients.
questions.hint: Find a pair whose sum is the negative of the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

questions.concept: Direct proportional scaling of runtime with workload size
questions.learningObjective: Solve a direct-proportion problem relating processing time to workload size.
questions.question: An algorithm processes \(8\) packets in \(10\) time-units. Its runtime is directly proportional to the number of packets. How long does it take to process \(12\) packets at the same rate?
questions.explanation: Time per item remains fixed, so the new time is \(10\cdot\frac{12}{8}=15\) time-units.
questions.hint: Scale the original time by the ratio of the new item count to the original item count.

questions.concept: Applying a proportional scale factor to a workload
questions.learningObjective: Apply a proportional scale factor directly to a workload quantity.
questions.question: A model's workload is directly proportional to input size. The current workload is \(45\) operations. If the input size is multiplied by \(4\), what is the new workload?
questions.explanation: Direct proportionality applies the same factor to the workload: \(45\cdot 4=180\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply the original workload by the input-size scale factor.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for linear search
questions.learningObjective: Recall the worst-case comparison count for a linear search over n elements.
questions.question: Linear search checks an unsorted array of \(n=334\) elements one at a time. Count one equality comparison between the target and each examined element. What is the worst-case comparison count when the target may be present or absent?
questions.explanation: If the target is absent, every element must be checked. If it is last, the same number of checks is needed. Thus the maximum is \(n=334\) key-to-element comparisons.
questions.hint: Consider a target that is absent or is the final element checked.

questions.concept: Counting combinations (unordered selections)
questions.learningObjective: Count unordered selections without replacement using combinations.
questions.question: A test suite chooses \(4\) distinct test cases from \(10\) available cases without replacement. Order does not matter. How many selections are possible?
questions.explanation: Count ordered choices, then remove the order of the selected group: \(\binom{10}{4}=\frac{10!}{4!(10-4)!}=210\).
questions.hint: Use unordered selections; each selected group has multiple orderings that should be counted only once.

questions.concept: Computing throughput from total items and elapsed time
questions.learningObjective: Compute throughput as items processed divided by elapsed time.
questions.question: A pipeline processes \(196\) requests in \(28\) seconds at a steady rate. What is its throughput in requests per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput is the number of processed items divided by elapsed time: \(\frac{196}{28}=7\) requests per second.
questions.hint: Divide the total number of processed items by the elapsed time.

questions.concept: Applying the handshake lemma to count edges from vertex degrees
questions.learningObjective: Use the handshake lemma on a realizable simple undirected graph.
questions.question: A simple undirected graph has \(9\) vertices with degree sequence \((8,8,8,6,5,6,6,5,4)\). How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: Each edge contributes one degree at each of its two endpoints. The degree sum is \(8+8+8+6+5+6+6+5+4=56\), so \(|E|=\frac{56}{2}=28\). The listed sequence has an explicit simple-graph realization, so this degree sum corresponds to a possible graph.
questions.hint: Count how often each edge is included when you add all vertex degrees.

questions.concept: Computing terms of a Fibonacci-style recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Compute terms of a two-term linear recurrence by direct iteration.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers, \(a_0=4\) and \(a_1=4\), while \(a_k=a_{k-1}+a_{k-2}\) for \(k\ge 2\). What is \(a_{6}\)?
questions.explanation:
Build each term from the previous two:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2}&=4+4=8\\
a_{3}&=8+4=12\\
a_{4}&=12+8=20\\
a_{5}&=20+12=32\\
a_{6}&=32+20=52
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(a_{6}=52\).
questions.hint: Start from the two given initial values and compute one new term at a time.

questions.concept: Computing a runtime after a percentage reduction
questions.learningObjective: Apply a percentage decrease to a runtime value.
questions.question: An optimization reduces a routine's runtime of \(140\) milliseconds by \(20\%\). What is the exact new runtime?
questions.explanation:
Apply the percentage exactly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{reduction}&=140\cdot\frac{20}{100}=28\\
\text{new runtime}&=140-28=112
\end{aligned}
\]
The new runtime is \(112\) milliseconds; no integer rounding is applied.
questions.hint: Multiply the original runtime by the fraction that remains after the reduction.

questions.concept: Computing a value modulo m for hash bucket assignment
questions.learningObjective: Apply the modulo operation to compute a hash bucket index.
questions.question: A hash table assigns key \(274\) to bucket \(274\bmod 18\). What is the bucket index, using remainders from \(0\) through \(17\)?
questions.explanation: Euclidean division gives \(274=18\cdot 15+4\). Since \(0\le 4<18\), the remainder and bucket index are \(4\).
questions.hint: Use the remainder, rather than the quotient, after division by the bucket count.

questions.concept: Bounding the length of a shortest simple path
questions.learningObjective: Prove and attain the largest possible shortest-path distance in a simple connected unweighted graph.
questions.question: Consider all simple connected undirected unweighted graphs on \(n=16\) vertices and all pairs of distinct vertices in them. What is the largest possible shortest-path length, measured in edges?
questions.explanation: A shortest path cannot repeat a vertex: removing a cycle would shorten it. It therefore visits at most \(16\) vertices and uses at most \(n-1=15\) edges. This bound is achieved by the two endpoints of a path graph on \(16\) vertices, so it is the largest possible value.
questions.hint: Use the no-repeated-vertex bound, then consider the endpoints of a graph that is itself a path.

questions.concept: Determining whether a number is prime
questions.learningObjective: Determine primality by checking for divisors up to the square root of the number.
questions.question: Which statement correctly classifies the integer \(41\) as prime or composite?

options.label: A
options.text: Prime: it has exactly two positive divisors.

options.label: B
options.text: Composite: it has more than two positive divisors.

questions.explanation: Any composite integer has a factor no larger than its square root. No integer from \(2\) through \(6\) divides \(41\) evenly. Since \(41\) exceeds \(1\), it is prime.
questions.hint: Try divisors up to the square root; one nontrivial divisor is enough to prove compositeness.

questions.concept: Counting edges in a complete graph
questions.learningObjective: Count the unordered vertex pairs of a simple undirected complete graph.
questions.question: How many edges are in a simple undirected complete graph with \(n=13\) vertices?
questions.explanation: Each edge joins one unordered pair of distinct vertices. Therefore, \(\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\). Substituting \(n=13\) gives \(\frac{13\cdot 12}{2}=78\).
questions.hint: Count unordered pairs of distinct vertices.

questions.concept: Identifying the complexity class of a quadratic model
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tight asymptotic class of a quadratic operation-count model.
questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=3n^2+4n+7\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n^2}=3+\frac{4}{n}+\frac{7}{n^2}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(3\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n^2)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.
questions.hint: Identify the highest power with a nonzero positive coefficient.

questions.concept: Counting permutations of a set of distinct items
questions.learningObjective: Recall and apply the factorial formula for counting permutations.
questions.question: An algorithm considers every ordering of \(14\) distinct tasks. How many orderings are possible?
questions.explanation: There are \(14\) choices for the first position, \(13\) for the next, and so on. The product is \(14!=\prod_{i=1}^{14}i=87178291200\).
questions.hint: Use the multiplication principle with one fewer available item at each new position.

questions.concept: Counting permutations of a set of distinct items
questions.learningObjective: Recall and apply the factorial formula for counting permutations.
questions.question: An algorithm considers every ordering of \(15\) distinct modules. How many orderings are possible?
questions.explanation: There are \(15\) choices for the first position, \(14\) for the next, and so on. The product is \(15!=\prod_{i=1}^{15}i=1307674368000\).
questions.hint: Use the multiplication principle with one fewer available item at each new position.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on cubic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a cubic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=7n^3\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(5\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?

Compare the new count with the original:

questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=3n^2+3n+2\) as \(n\to\infty\)?

questions.explanation: Each edge joins one unordered pair of distinct vertices. Therefore, \(\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\). Substituting \(n=7\) gives \(\frac{7\cdot 6}{2}=21\).

questions.concept: Determining whether a number is prime
questions.learningObjective: Determine primality by checking for divisors up to the square root of the number.
questions.question: Which statement correctly classifies the integer \(91\) as prime or composite?

options.label: A
options.text: Prime: its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(91\).

questions.explanation: The number has a nontrivial divisor: \(91=7\cdot 13\). Both factors exceed \(1\), so the number is composite.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes (largest case)
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=100001\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the largest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the largest expression is \(n^2\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Direct proportional scaling of runtime with workload size
questions.learningObjective: Solve a direct-proportion problem relating processing time to workload size.
questions.question: An algorithm processes \(21\) packets in \(20\) seconds. Its runtime is directly proportional to the number of packets. How long does it take to process \(2\) packets at the same rate?
questions.explanation: Time per item remains fixed, so the new time is \(20\cdot\frac{2}{21}=\frac{40}{21}\) seconds.
questions.hint: Scale the original time by the ratio of the new item count to the original item count.

questions.learningObjective: Recall the worst-case comparison count for a linear search over n elements.
questions.question: Linear search checks an unsorted array of \(n=486\) elements one at a time. Count one equality comparison between the target and each examined element. What is the worst-case comparison count when the target may be present or absent?
questions.explanation: If the target is absent, every element must be checked. If it is last, the same number of checks is needed. Thus the maximum is \(n=486\) key-to-element comparisons.

questions.concept: Interpreting an amortized cost bound
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what an amortized per-operation bound implies about total cost over many operations.
questions.question: Starting from an empty dynamic array, a resizing policy guarantees that the total number of element-copy operations over \(63\) insertions is at most \(5\) times the number of insertions. What is the smallest total upper bound supplied by this guarantee alone?
questions.explanation: Apply the given aggregate guarantee: \(5\cdot 63=315\) element-copy operations. This is an upper bound on the entire sequence; an individual insertion may copy more than \(5\) elements.
questions.hint: Apply the stated bound to the entire insertion sequence, rather than to one worst-case insertion.

questions.concept: Counting steps in the Euclidean algorithm
questions.learningObjective: Trace the Euclidean algorithm to count the number of division steps to compute a GCD.
questions.question: Starting with \((98,57)\), run the Euclidean algorithm to compute \(\gcd(98,57)\). Count every remainder-producing division, including the final division whose remainder is zero. How many division steps are required?
questions.explanation:
The divisions are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
98&=1\cdot 57+41\\
57&=1\cdot 41+16\\
41&=2\cdot 16+9\\
16&=1\cdot 9+7\\
9&=1\cdot 7+2\\
7&=3\cdot 2+1\\
2&=2\cdot 1+0
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(7\) divisions, including the final zero-remainder division. The last nonzero remainder (or divisor at termination) is \(1\), the greatest common divisor.
questions.hint: Record one step for each computed remainder, and include the step that produces zero.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for binary search
questions.learningObjective: Count worst-case key-to-element comparisons in a specified standard binary-search implementation.
questions.question: Standard binary search examines a sorted array of \(n=8\) distinct elements. It uses an inclusive index interval, chooses the lower middle index, and removes the middle element after an unequal comparison. Count one three-way key-to-element comparison per examined element; exclude index and loop-condition checks. What is the maximum number of these comparisons over all present or absent targets?
questions.explanation: The worst remaining interval after one comparison has \(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor\) elements. Hence \(C(0)=0\) and \(C(n)=1+C(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor)\) for \(n\ge 1\). Repeated halving until the interval is empty gives \(C(n)=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\). For this array, \(C(8)=\lfloor\log_2 8\rfloor+1=4\).
questions.hint: Include the comparison with the final remaining element; stopping when only one candidate remains can miss a comparison.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes (largest case)
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=500\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the largest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the largest expression is \(n^2\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Computing a net workload reduction (delta)
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a net change (delta) between two workload measurements, including its direction.
questions.question: Caching reduces a service's operation count from \(829\) to \(676\) operations per request. By how many operations per request does the count decrease?
questions.explanation: The reduction is the original count minus the new count: \(829-676=153\) operations per request. This positive reduction measures the size of the decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the new count from the original count.

questions.concept: Counting leaves in a recursion tree
questions.learningObjective: Count the number of base-case invocations in a recursion tree with a fixed branching factor and depth.
questions.question: The root call is at depth \(0\). Every call at a depth less than \(6\) makes exactly \(2\) child calls, and all calls at depth \(6\) are base cases. How many base-case calls are made?
questions.explanation: The number of calls starts at \(1\) and is multiplied by \(2\) at each depth. At depth \(6\), the leaf count is \(2^{6}=64\).
questions.hint: Count one branching multiplication for each edge-depth between the root and a leaf.

questions.concept: Counting the total number of subsets of a set
questions.learningObjective: Count all subsets by independent inclusion and exclusion choices.
questions.question: How many subsets, including the empty set and the full set, does a set of \(3\) distinct elements have?
questions.explanation: For each element there are two independent choices: include it or exclude it. By the multiplication principle, \(2^{3}=8\) subsets are possible.
questions.hint: Assign each element one of two inclusion states, then count all state combinations.

questions.concept: Applying the Master Theorem to classify a recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Apply the Master Theorem, including the regularity condition when needed, without rounding critical exponents.
questions.question: For \(n=2^k\) with nonnegative integer \(k\), suppose \(T(1)=1\) and \(T(n)=4T\!\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)+n^2\) for \(n>1\). Which Master Theorem case and tight asymptotic bound apply?
questions.explanation: Because \(4=2^{2}\), the critical exponent is \(\log_{2}4=2\). The combine cost matches \(n^{\log_{2}4}\), so Case \(2\) gives \(T(n)=\Theta(n^2\log n)\).
questions.hint: Compare the branching factor with the shrink factor raised to the combine-cost exponent; for combine-cost dominance, also check regularity.

questions.concept: Applying the handshake lemma to count edges from vertex degrees
questions.learningObjective: Use the handshake lemma on a realizable simple undirected graph.
questions.question: A simple undirected graph has \(11\) vertices with degree sequence \((7,6,7,8,4,4,10,9,2,4,5)\). How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: Each edge contributes one degree at each of its two endpoints. The degree sum is \(7+6+7+8+4+4+10+9+2+4+5=66\), so \(|E|=\frac{66}{2}=33\). The listed sequence has an explicit simple-graph realization, so this degree sum corresponds to a possible graph.

questions.concept: Computing a basic probability as favorable over total outcomes
questions.learningObjective: Apply the basic probability formula: favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
questions.question: A test harness chooses one case uniformly at random from \(33\) cases, of which \(30\) fail. What is the probability of choosing a failing case?
questions.explanation: All cases are equally likely, so \(P(\text{failure})=\frac{30}{33}=\frac{10}{11}\).
questions.hint: Use the number of failing cases divided by the total number of cases.

questions.concept: Recovering input size from a linear operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Solve a two-step linear equation to recover an algorithm's input size from a measured operation count.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=7n+25\). One run uses \(200\) operations. What is its nonnegative integer input size \(n\)?
questions.explanation:
Undo the fixed cost, then divide by the coefficient:
\[
\begin{aligned}
7n&=200-25=175\\
n&=\frac{175}{7}=25
\end{aligned}
\]
Checking gives \(7\cdot 25+25=200\).
questions.hint: Remove the fixed overhead before dividing by the per-element cost.

questions.question: At input size \(n=500\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the smallest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).

The divisions are:

\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(3\) divisions, including the final zero-remainder division. The last nonzero remainder (or divisor at termination) is \(1\), the greatest common divisor.
questions.hint: Record one step for each computed remainder, and include the step that produces zero.

a_{3}&=8+5=13\\
a_{4}&=13+8=21\\
a_{5}&=21+13=34
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(a_{5}=34\).

questions.concept: Solving a shared-workload equation with algebraic fractions
questions.learningObjective: Clear algebraic fractions to solve for a total workload split across two processes.
questions.question: A workload contains \(n\) items. In one round, two processes handle disjoint parts: the first processes \(\frac{n}{2}\) items and the second processes \(\frac{n}{5}\) items. Together they process \(21\) items in that round; the rest remain for later. What is the total workload \(n\)?
questions.explanation:
Add the two disjoint processed parts:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{n}{2}+\frac{n}{5}&=21\\
7n&=210\\
n&=30
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution gives \(15\) items for the first process and \(6\) for the second, totaling \(21\).
questions.hint: Add the two fractional portions, then clear the denominators.

questions.concept: Computing a value modulo m for hash bucket assignment
questions.learningObjective: Apply the modulo operation to compute a hash bucket index.
questions.question: A hash table assigns key \(187\) to bucket \(187\bmod 4\). What is the bucket index, using remainders from \(0\) through \(3\)?
questions.explanation: Euclidean division gives \(187=4\cdot 46+3\). Since \(0\le 3<4\), the remainder and bucket index are \(3\).
questions.hint: Use the remainder, rather than the quotient, after division by the bucket count.

questions.concept: Applying a proportional scale factor to a workload
questions.learningObjective: Apply a proportional scale factor directly to a workload quantity.
questions.question: A model's workload is directly proportional to input size. The current workload is \(35\) operations. If the input size is multiplied by \(2\), what is the new workload?
questions.explanation: Direct proportionality applies the same factor to the workload: \(35\cdot 2=70\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply the original workload by the input-size scale factor.

questions.concept: Applying the Master Theorem to classify a recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Apply the Master Theorem, including the regularity condition when needed, without rounding critical exponents.
questions.question: For \(n=3^k\) with nonnegative integer \(k\), suppose \(T(1)=1\) and \(T(n)=4T\!\left(\frac{n}{3}\right)+1\) for \(n>1\). Which Master Theorem case and tight asymptotic bound apply?
questions.explanation: Here \(a=4\), \(b=3\), and \(f(n)=1\). Because \(4>3^{0}\), \(\log_{3}4>0\). Choose \(\varepsilon=\frac{\log_{3}4-0}{2}>0\); then \(f(n)=O(n^{\log_{3}4-\varepsilon})\). Case \(1\) applies, giving \(T(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_{3}4})\).
questions.hint: Compare the branching factor with the shrink factor raised to the combine-cost exponent; for combine-cost dominance, also check regularity.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on quadratic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a quadratic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=5n^2\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(4\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?
questions.explanation:
Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T(4n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{5(4n)^2}{5n^2}\\
&=4^2=16
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(16\).
questions.hint: Substitute the scaled input and form the ratio of the new model to the original.

questions.concept: Summing sequential pipeline stage runtimes
questions.learningObjective: Sum the runtimes of sequential pipeline stages to find total processing time.
questions.question: One item passes through \(5\) sequential pipeline stages taking \(8\), \(7\), \(17\), \(11\), \(10\) milliseconds, respectively. The item incurs no other delay, and its stages do not overlap. What is its total processing time?
questions.explanation: Add the sequential stage durations: \(8+7+17+11+10=53\) milliseconds.
questions.hint: The same item completes each stage before starting the next.

questions.concept: Counting leaves in a recursion tree
questions.learningObjective: Count the number of base-case invocations in a recursion tree with a fixed branching factor and depth.
questions.question: The root call is at depth \(0\). Every call at a depth less than \(4\) makes exactly \(4\) child calls, and all calls at depth \(4\) are base cases. How many base-case calls are made?
questions.explanation: The number of calls starts at \(1\) and is multiplied by \(4\) at each depth. At depth \(4\), the leaf count is \(4^{4}=256\).
questions.hint: Count one branching multiplication for each edge-depth between the root and a leaf.

questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a quadratic time-complexity model with quadratic, linear, and constant terms for a given input size.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=4n^2+2n+5\). How many operations are performed when \(n=9\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute and compute the square first:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(9)&=4\cdot 9^2+2\cdot 9+5\\
&=324+18+5=347
\end{aligned}
\]
The count is \(347\) operations.
questions.hint: Square the input size before multiplying by the leading coefficient.

questions.concept: Bounding the length of a shortest simple path
questions.learningObjective: Prove and attain the largest possible shortest-path distance in a simple connected unweighted graph.
questions.question: Consider all simple connected undirected unweighted graphs on \(n=18\) vertices and all pairs of distinct vertices in them. What is the largest possible shortest-path length, measured in edges?
questions.explanation: A shortest path cannot repeat a vertex: removing a cycle would shorten it. It therefore visits at most \(18\) vertices and uses at most \(n-1=17\) edges. This bound is achieved by the two endpoints of a path graph on \(18\) vertices, so it is the largest possible value.
questions.hint: Use the no-repeated-vertex bound, then consider the endpoints of a graph that is itself a path.

questions.concept: Solving the characteristic equation of a linear recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Solve a quadratic characteristic equation associated with a linear recurrence relation.
questions.question: A linear recurrence has the characteristic equation \(x^2+3x-10=0\). What are its two roots?
questions.explanation:
Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2+3x-10&=(x+5)(x-2)\\
(x+5)(x-2)&=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-5\) and \(x=2\). Their sum is \(-5+2=-3\) and their product is \((-5)(2)=-10\), matching the coefficients.
questions.hint: Find a pair whose sum is the negative of the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes (largest case)
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=1000001\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the largest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the largest expression is \(n^2\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a cubic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=3n^3\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(5\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?

questions.concept: Computing geometric growth over repeated rounds
questions.learningObjective: Apply the geometric growth repeated-multiplication model.
questions.question: A crawler starts with \(28\) discovered pages at round \(0\). Its discovered-page count is multiplied by \(2\) at the end of every round. How many pages are counted after \(6\) rounds?
questions.explanation: The growth factor is applied once per round: \(28\cdot 2^{6}=28\cdot 64=1792\) pages.
questions.hint: Use one multiplication by the growth factor for each completed round.

questions.concept: Bounding the length of a shortest simple path
questions.learningObjective: Prove and attain the largest possible shortest-path distance in a simple connected unweighted graph.
questions.question: Consider all simple connected undirected unweighted graphs on \(n=8\) vertices and all pairs of distinct vertices in them. What is the largest possible shortest-path length, measured in edges?
questions.explanation: A shortest path cannot repeat a vertex: removing a cycle would shorten it. It therefore visits at most \(8\) vertices and uses at most \(n-1=7\) edges. This bound is achieved by the two endpoints of a path graph on \(8\) vertices, so it is the largest possible value.

questions.concept: Determining whether a number is prime
questions.learningObjective: Determine primality by checking for divisors up to the square root of the number.
questions.question: Which statement correctly classifies the integer \(51\) as prime or composite?

options.label: A
options.text: Prime: its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(51\).

questions.explanation: The number has a nontrivial divisor: \(51=3\cdot 17\). Both factors exceed \(1\), so the number is composite.
questions.hint: Try divisors up to the square root; one nontrivial divisor is enough to prove compositeness.

questions.concept: Recovering input size from a linear operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Solve a two-step linear equation to recover an algorithm's input size from a measured operation count.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=5n+14\). One run uses \(39\) operations. What is its nonnegative integer input size \(n\)?
questions.explanation:
Undo the fixed cost, then divide by the coefficient:
\[
\begin{aligned}
5n&=39-14=25\\
n&=\frac{25}{5}=5
\end{aligned}
\]
Checking gives \(5\cdot 5+14=39\).
questions.hint: Remove the fixed overhead before dividing by the per-element cost.

questions.concept: Identifying the complexity class of a quadratic model
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tight asymptotic class of a quadratic operation-count model.
questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=3n^2+3n+6\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n^2}=3+\frac{3}{n}+\frac{6}{n^2}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(3\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n^2)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.
questions.hint: Identify the highest power with a nonzero positive coefficient.

questions.concept: Applying the tree edge-count property
questions.learningObjective: Use the edge-count property of a finite tree.
questions.question: A spanning tree connects \(n=59\) vertices of a connected undirected network. How many edges does the tree contain?
questions.explanation: A tree with \(n\) vertices has exactly \(n-1\) edges. Starting with one root, each of the remaining vertices adds one edge to its parent. Here, \(59-1=58\).
questions.hint: In a tree, each vertex other than the root has one edge to its parent.

questions.concept: Computing a runtime after a percentage reduction
questions.learningObjective: Apply a percentage decrease to a runtime value.
questions.question: An optimization reduces a routine's runtime of \(55\) milliseconds by \(30\%\). What is the exact new runtime?
questions.explanation:
Apply the percentage exactly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{reduction}&=55\cdot\frac{30}{100}=16.5\\
\text{new runtime}&=55-16.5=38.5
\end{aligned}
\]
The new runtime is \(38.5\) milliseconds; no integer rounding is applied.
questions.hint: Multiply the original runtime by the fraction that remains after the reduction.

questions.concept: Evaluating a linear operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a linear time-complexity model with a fixed cost and a per-element cost for a given input size.
questions.question: An algorithm has the exact operation-count model \(T(n)=7n+12\). How many operations does it perform when \(n=20\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute the input size: \(T(20)=7\cdot 20+12=152\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply by the per-element coefficient, then add the fixed overhead.

questions.concept: Identifying the complexity class of a quadratic model
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tight asymptotic class of a quadratic operation-count model.
questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=2n^2+3n+1\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n^2}=2+\frac{3}{n}+\frac{1}{n^2}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(2\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n^2)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.

questions.concept: Direct proportional scaling of runtime with workload size
questions.learningObjective: Solve a direct-proportion problem relating processing time to workload size.
questions.question: An algorithm processes \(25\) records in \(15\) milliseconds. Its runtime is directly proportional to the number of records. How long does it take to process \(11\) records at the same rate?
questions.explanation: Time per item remains fixed, so the new time is \(15\cdot\frac{11}{25}=6.6\) milliseconds.
questions.hint: Scale the original time by the ratio of the new item count to the original item count.

questions.concept: Summing sequential pipeline stage runtimes

questions.question: One item passes through \(3\) sequential pipeline stages taking \(3\), \(25\), \(15\) milliseconds, respectively. The item incurs no other delay, and its stages do not overlap. What is its total processing time?
questions.explanation: Add the sequential stage durations: \(3+25+15=43\) milliseconds.
questions.hint: The same item completes each stage before starting the next.

questions.concept: Computing a value modulo m for hash bucket assignment
questions.learningObjective: Apply the modulo operation to compute a hash bucket index.
questions.question: A hash table assigns key \(158\) to bucket \(158\bmod 8\). What is the bucket index, using remainders from \(0\) through \(7\)?
questions.explanation: Euclidean division gives \(158=8\cdot 19+6\). Since \(0\le 6<8\), the remainder and bucket index are \(6\).
questions.hint: Use the remainder, rather than the quotient, after division by the bucket count.

questions.concept: Identifying the complexity class of a quadratic model
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tight asymptotic class of a quadratic operation-count model.
questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=3n^2+6n+16\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n^2}=3+\frac{6}{n}+\frac{16}{n^2}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(3\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n^2)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.
questions.hint: Identify the highest power with a nonzero positive coefficient.

questions.concept: Computing throughput from total items and elapsed time
questions.learningObjective: Compute throughput as items processed divided by elapsed time.
questions.question: A pipeline processes \(756\) tiles in \(18\) seconds at a steady rate. What is its throughput in tiles per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput is the number of processed items divided by elapsed time: \(\frac{756}{18}=42\) tiles per second.
questions.hint: Divide the total number of processed items by the elapsed time.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for binary search
questions.learningObjective: Count worst-case key-to-element comparisons in a specified standard binary-search implementation.
questions.question: Standard binary search examines a sorted array of \(n=129\) distinct elements. It uses an inclusive index interval, chooses the lower middle index, and removes the middle element after an unequal comparison. Count one three-way key-to-element comparison per examined element; exclude index and loop-condition checks. What is the maximum number of these comparisons over all present or absent targets?
questions.explanation: The worst remaining interval after one comparison has \(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor\) elements. Hence \(C(0)=0\) and \(C(n)=1+C(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor)\) for \(n\ge 1\). Repeated halving until the interval is empty gives \(C(n)=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\). For this array, \(C(129)=\lfloor\log_2 129\rfloor+1=8\).
questions.hint: Include the comparison with the final remaining element; stopping when only one candidate remains can miss a comparison.

questions.concept: Computing a runtime after a percentage reduction
questions.learningObjective: Apply a percentage decrease to a runtime value.
questions.question: An optimization reduces a routine's runtime of \(239\) milliseconds by \(40\%\). What is the exact new runtime?
questions.explanation:
Apply the percentage exactly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{reduction}&=239\cdot\frac{40}{100}=95.6\\
\text{new runtime}&=239-95.6=143.4
\end{aligned}
\]
The new runtime is \(143.4\) milliseconds; no integer rounding is applied.
questions.hint: Multiply the original runtime by the fraction that remains after the reduction.

questions.concept: Computing a net workload reduction (delta)
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a net change (delta) between two workload measurements, including its direction.
questions.question: Caching reduces a service's operation count from \(362\) to \(175\) operations per request. By how many operations per request does the count decrease?
questions.explanation: The reduction is the original count minus the new count: \(362-175=187\) operations per request. This positive reduction measures the size of the decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the new count from the original count.

questions.concept: Computing expected trials until first success (geometric distribution)
questions.learningObjective: Compute the expected number of independent trials up to and including the first success.
questions.question: An algorithm succeeds on each attempt independently with the same probability \(p=\frac{1}{9}\). Let \(X\) count all attempts up to and including the first success. What is \(\mathbb{E}[X]\)?
questions.explanation: One attempt is always made. With probability \(1-p\), a failure leaves the same expected number of additional attempts. Thus \(\mathbb{E}[X]=1+(1-p)\mathbb{E}[X]\), which gives \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{1}{p}=9\). The first successful attempt is included.
questions.hint: After a failed attempt, the remaining task has the same distribution as at the start.

questions.concept: Expressing a workload change as a signed delta
questions.learningObjective: Correctly interpret a negative signed delta as a decrease, distinct from a negative operation count.
questions.question: A refactor changes a function's operation count from \(105\) to \(19\) operations per call. Define the signed change as \(\Delta=\text{new}-\text{original}\). What is \(\Delta\)?
questions.explanation: Using the specified sign convention, \(\Delta=19-105=-86\) operations per call. The negative sign denotes a decrease; the new operation count itself is \(19\) and remains nonnegative.
questions.hint: Use the stated order of subtraction, and let the sign show the direction of change.

questions.concept: Applying the pigeonhole principle to guarantee a minimum bin size
questions.learningObjective: Apply the pigeonhole principle's ceiling-division bound.
questions.question: \(8\) items are distributed among \(7\) labeled bins. What is the largest integer \(L\) such that every distribution guarantees at least one bin containing \(L\) or more items?
questions.explanation: If every bin held at most \(1\) items, the total would be at most \(7\cdot 1=7\), which is less than \(8\). Therefore some bin has at least \(\left\lceil\frac{8}{7}\right\rceil=2\) items. Distributing the items as evenly as possible attains this largest-bin size, so no stronger guarantee is possible.
questions.hint: Find the ceiling of the average bin size, then check an even distribution to see whether the bound is sharp.

questions.concept: Computing amortized per-item cost for a batch operation
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish per-item cost from amortized cost, which spreads the fixed overhead across the whole batch.
questions.question: A batch has a fixed overhead of \(20\) operations and an additional \(3\) operations per item. For a batch of \(47\) items, what is the average number of operations per item? Round the final average to two decimal places when needed.
questions.explanation:
Add the overhead to the total item cost, then average:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{total}&=20+3\cdot 47=161\\
\text{average}&=\frac{161}{47}\approx 3.43
\end{aligned}
\]
The result is \(3.43\) operations per item. The fixed overhead is spread across the entire batch.
questions.hint: First find the total batch cost, including overhead; then divide by the number of items.

questions.learningObjective: Correctly interpret a negative signed delta as a decrease, distinct from a negative operation count.

questions.concept: Applying the handshake lemma to count edges from vertex degrees
questions.learningObjective: Use the handshake lemma on a realizable simple undirected graph.
questions.question: A simple undirected graph has \(4\) vertices with degree sequence \((2,2,2,2)\). How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: Each edge contributes one degree at each of its two endpoints. The degree sum is \(2+2+2+2=8\), so \(|E|=\frac{8}{2}=4\). The listed sequence has an explicit simple-graph realization, so this degree sum corresponds to a possible graph.
questions.hint: Count how often each edge is included when you add all vertex degrees.

questions.concept: Applying the pigeonhole principle to guarantee a minimum bin size
questions.learningObjective: Apply the pigeonhole principle's ceiling-division bound.
questions.question: \(24\) items are distributed among \(13\) labeled bins. What is the largest integer \(L\) such that every distribution guarantees at least one bin containing \(L\) or more items?
questions.explanation: If every bin held at most \(1\) items, the total would be at most \(13\cdot 1=13\), which is less than \(24\). Therefore some bin has at least \(\left\lceil\frac{24}{13}\right\rceil=2\) items. Distributing the items as evenly as possible attains this largest-bin size, so no stronger guarantee is possible.
questions.hint: Find the ceiling of the average bin size, then check an even distribution to see whether the bound is sharp.

questions.concept: Computing throughput from total items and elapsed time

questions.question: A pipeline processes \(1653\) transactions in \(19\) seconds at a steady rate. What is its throughput in transactions per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput is the number of processed items divided by elapsed time: \(\frac{1653}{19}=87\) transactions per second.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for binary search

questions.question: Standard binary search examines a sorted array of \(n=513\) distinct elements. questions.explanation: The worst remaining interval after one comparison has \(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor\) elements. Hence \(C(0)=0\) and \(C(n)=1+C(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor)\) for \(n\ge 1\). Repeated halving until the interval is empty gives \(C(n)=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\). For this array, \(C(513)=\lfloor\log_2 513\rfloor+1=10\).

\end{aligned}

questions.concept: Computing amortized per-item cost for a batch operation

questions.question: A batch has a fixed overhead of \(33\) operations and an additional \(3\) operations per item. For a batch of \(42\) items, what is the average number of operations per item? Round the final average to two decimal places when needed.
questions.explanation:
Add the overhead to the total item cost, then average:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{total}&=33+3\cdot 42=159\\
\text{average}&=\frac{159}{42}\approx 3.79
\end{aligned}
\]
The result is \(3.79\) operations per item. The fixed overhead is spread across the entire batch.

questions.explanation: The reduction is the original count minus the new count: \(829-198=631\) operations per request. This positive reduction measures the size of the decrease.

questions.concept: Applying the Master Theorem to classify a recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Apply the Master Theorem, including the regularity condition when needed, without rounding critical exponents.
questions.question: For \(n=3^k\) with nonnegative integer \(k\), suppose \(T(1)=1\) and \(T(n)=2T\!\left(\frac{n}{3}\right)+n\) for \(n>1\). Which Master Theorem case and tight asymptotic bound apply?
questions.explanation: Because \(2<3^{1}\), \(1>\log_{3}2\). Thus the combine cost is polynomially larger than the critical term. The regularity condition holds: \(a f(\frac{n}{b})=\frac{2}{3^{1}}f(n)\), with \(c=\frac{2}{3^{1}}<1\). Therefore Case \(3\) gives \(T(n)=\Theta(n)\).
questions.hint: Compare the branching factor with the shrink factor raised to the combine-cost exponent; for combine-cost dominance, also check regularity.

questions.concept: Applying the handshake lemma to count edges from vertex degrees

questions.question: A simple undirected graph has \(11\) vertices with degree sequence \((10,10,10,5,5,6,5,5,5,5,4)\). How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: Each edge contributes one degree at each of its two endpoints. The degree sum is \(10+10+10+5+5+6+5+5+5+5+4=70\), so \(|E|=\frac{70}{2}=35\). The listed sequence has an explicit simple-graph realization, so this degree sum corresponds to a possible graph.
questions.hint: Count how often each edge is included when you add all vertex degrees.

questions.explanation: One attempt is always made. With probability \(1-p\), a failure leaves the same expected number of additional attempts. Thus \(\mathbb{E}[X]=1+(1-p)\mathbb{E}[X]\), which gives \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{1}{p}=12\). The first successful attempt is included.
