\begin{aligned}
T(6)&=4\cdot 6^2+2\cdot 6+13\\
&=144+12+13=169
\end{aligned}
\]
The count is \(169\) operations.
questions.hint: Square the input size before multiplying by the leading coefficient.

questions.concept: Distinguishing recursive and iterative algorithm structures
questions.learningObjective: Understand the structural requirements and behavior of recursion versus iteration.
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the usual structural distinction between recursion and iteration?

options.label: A
options.text: Recursion repeats work through self-calls, directly or indirectly; iteration repeats work through a loop.

options.label: B
options.text: Recursion always runs faster than iteration for the same task.

options.label: C
options.text: An iterative procedure cannot use a stopping condition, and a recursive procedure cannot use variables.

questions.explanation: A recursive procedure repeats work through calls to itself, directly or indirectly; an iterative procedure repeats work through a loop. Both require appropriate stopping logic. Neither structure alone guarantees faster execution.
questions.hint: Focus on the mechanism used to repeat work, rather than assuming a performance advantage.

questions.concept: Computing a term of a geometric sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute a requested term from the first term and common ratio of a geometric sequence.
questions.question: A geometric sequence has \(a_1=2\) and common ratio \(2\). What is \(a_{3}\)?
questions.explanation: The first term is multiplied by the common ratio \(2\) times to reach term \(3\): \(a_{3}=2\cdot 2^{2}=8\).
questions.hint: The exponent is one less than the index of the requested term.

questions.concept: Counting steps in the Euclidean algorithm
questions.learningObjective: Trace the Euclidean algorithm to count the number of division steps to compute a GCD.
questions.question: Starting with \((49,35)\), run the Euclidean algorithm to compute \(\gcd(49,35)\). Count every remainder-producing division, including the final division whose remainder is zero. How many division steps are required?
questions.explanation:
The divisions are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
49&=1\cdot 35+14\\
35&=2\cdot 14+7\\
14&=2\cdot 7+0
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(3\) divisions, including the final zero-remainder division. The last nonzero remainder (or divisor at termination) is \(7\), the greatest common divisor.
questions.hint: Record one step for each computed remainder, and include the step that produces zero.

questions.concept: Inverse proportional scaling of time with number of workers
questions.learningObjective: Solve an inverse-proportion problem relating completion time to the number of parallel workers.
questions.question: A fixed job takes \(34\) minutes with \(6\) identical workers. Assume all work is perfectly divisible, all workers run at the same constant rate, and there is no communication, setup, or sequential overhead. How long does the job take with \(2\) workers?
questions.explanation: The required worker-time is fixed: \(6\cdot 34=204\) worker-minutes. Dividing by the new worker count gives \(\frac{204}{2}=102\) minutes.
questions.hint: Keep the product of the worker count and completion time constant.

questions.concept: Applying the Master Theorem to classify a recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Apply the Master Theorem, including the regularity condition when needed, without rounding critical exponents.
questions.question: For \(n=2^k\) with nonnegative integer \(k\), suppose \(T(1)=1\) and \(T(n)=2T\!\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)+n\) for \(n>1\). Which Master Theorem case and tight asymptotic bound apply?
questions.explanation: Because \(2=2^{1}\), the critical exponent is \(\log_{2}2=1\). The combine cost matches \(n^{\log_{2}2}\), so Case \(2\) gives \(T(n)=\Theta(n\log n)\).
questions.hint: Compare the branching factor with the shrink factor raised to the combine-cost exponent; for combine-cost dominance, also check regularity.

questions.concept: Counting nodes discovered at a given BFS layer
questions.learningObjective: Count nodes at a given BFS layer in a uniformly branching tree.
questions.question: Breadth-first search explores a rooted tree through layer \(2\). The root is layer \(0\), and every vertex in an earlier layer has exactly \(3\) distinct children. How many vertices are in layer \(2\)?
questions.explanation: A tree gives every child exactly one parent, so no vertices are shared between branches. The layer size is multiplied by \(3\) at each step, giving \(3^{2}=9\) vertices.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of vertices by the branching factor once per layer.

questions.concept: Computing geometric growth over repeated rounds
questions.learningObjective: Apply the geometric growth repeated-multiplication model.
questions.question: A crawler starts with \(44\) discovered pages at round \(0\). Its discovered-page count is multiplied by \(3\) at the end of every round. How many pages are counted after \(5\) rounds?
questions.explanation: The growth factor is applied once per round: \(44\cdot 3^{5}=44\cdot 243=10692\) pages.
questions.hint: Use one multiplication by the growth factor for each completed round.

questions.concept: Direct proportional scaling of runtime with workload size
questions.learningObjective: Solve a direct-proportion problem relating processing time to workload size.
questions.question: An algorithm processes \(9\) images in \(16\) time-units. Its runtime is directly proportional to the number of images. How long does it take to process \(26\) images at the same rate?
questions.explanation: Time per item remains fixed, so the new time is \(16\cdot\frac{26}{9}=\frac{416}{9}\) time-units.
questions.hint: Scale the original time by the ratio of the new item count to the original item count.

questions.concept: Solving a simple multiplicative recurrence by unrolling
questions.learningObjective: Solve a linear recurrence with a fixed multiplicative factor by unrolling it to the base case.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers \(n\), \(T(0)=1\) and \(T(n)=3T(n-1)\) for \(n\ge 1\). What is \(T(5)\)?
questions.explanation: Apply the multiplier \(3\) once for each of \(5\) steps: \(T(5)=1\cdot 3^{5}=243\).
questions.hint: Start with the base value and count one multiplication per recurrence step.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on cubic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a cubic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=7n^3\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(4\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?
questions.explanation:
Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T(4n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{7(4n)^3}{7n^3}\\
&=4^3=64
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(64\).
questions.hint: Substitute the scaled input and form the ratio of the new model to the original.

questions.concept: Computing expected trials until first success (geometric distribution)
questions.learningObjective: Compute the expected number of independent trials up to and including the first success.
questions.question: An algorithm succeeds on each attempt independently with the same probability \(p=\frac{1}{4}\). Let \(X\) count all attempts up to and including the first success. What is \(\mathbb{E}[X]\)?
questions.explanation: One attempt is always made. With probability \(1-p\), a failure leaves the same expected number of additional attempts. Thus \(\mathbb{E}[X]=1+(1-p)\mathbb{E}[X]\), which gives \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{1}{p}=4\). The first successful attempt is included.
questions.hint: After a failed attempt, the remaining task has the same distribution as at the start.

questions.concept: Identifying the complexity class of a quadratic model
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tight asymptotic class of a quadratic operation-count model.
questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=4n^2+8n+18\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n^2}=4+\frac{8}{n}+\frac{18}{n^2}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(4\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n^2)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.
questions.hint: Identify the highest power with a nonzero positive coefficient.

questions.concept: Bounding the length of a shortest simple path
questions.learningObjective: Prove and attain the largest possible shortest-path distance in a simple connected unweighted graph.
questions.question: Consider all simple connected undirected unweighted graphs on \(n=19\) vertices and all pairs of distinct vertices in them. What is the largest possible shortest-path length, measured in edges?
questions.explanation: A shortest path cannot repeat a vertex: removing a cycle would shorten it. It therefore visits at most \(19\) vertices and uses at most \(n-1=18\) edges. This bound is achieved by the two endpoints of a path graph on \(19\) vertices, so it is the largest possible value.
questions.hint: Use the no-repeated-vertex bound, then consider the endpoints of a graph that is itself a path.

questions.concept: Evaluating a linear operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a linear time-complexity model with a fixed cost and a per-element cost for a given input size.
questions.question: An algorithm has the exact operation-count model \(T(n)=3n+12\). How many operations does it perform when \(n=6\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute the input size: \(T(6)=3\cdot 6+12=30\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply by the per-element coefficient, then add the fixed overhead.

questions.concept: Bounding the length of a shortest simple path
questions.learningObjective: Prove and attain the largest possible shortest-path distance in a simple connected unweighted graph.
questions.question: Consider all simple connected undirected unweighted graphs on \(n=11\) vertices and all pairs of distinct vertices in them. What is the largest possible shortest-path length, measured in edges?
questions.explanation: A shortest path cannot repeat a vertex: removing a cycle would shorten it. It therefore visits at most \(11\) vertices and uses at most \(n-1=10\) edges. This bound is achieved by the two endpoints of a path graph on \(11\) vertices, so it is the largest possible value.
questions.hint: Use the no-repeated-vertex bound, then consider the endpoints of a graph that is itself a path.

questions.concept: Applying the pigeonhole principle to guarantee a minimum bin size
questions.learningObjective: Apply the pigeonhole principle's ceiling-division bound.
questions.question: \(10\) items are distributed among \(4\) labeled bins. What is the largest integer \(L\) such that every distribution guarantees at least one bin containing \(L\) or more items?
questions.explanation: If every bin held at most \(2\) items, the total would be at most \(4\cdot 2=8\), which is less than \(10\). Therefore some bin has at least \(\left\lceil\frac{10}{4}\right\rceil=3\) items. Distributing the items as evenly as possible attains this largest-bin size, so no stronger guarantee is possible.
questions.hint: Find the ceiling of the average bin size, then check an even distribution to see whether the bound is sharp.

questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a quadratic time-complexity model with quadratic, linear, and constant terms for a given input size.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=4n^2+6n+10\). How many operations are performed when \(n=8\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute and compute the square first:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(8)&=4\cdot 8^2+6\cdot 8+10\\
&=256+48+10=314
\end{aligned}
\]
The count is \(314\) operations.
questions.hint: Square the input size before multiplying by the leading coefficient.

questions.concept: Computing throughput from total items and elapsed time
questions.learningObjective: Compute throughput as items processed divided by elapsed time.
questions.question: A pipeline processes \(256\) records in \(32\) seconds at a steady rate. What is its throughput in records per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput is the number of processed items divided by elapsed time: \(\frac{256}{32}=8\) records per second.
questions.hint: Divide the total number of processed items by the elapsed time.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes (largest case)
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=503\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the largest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the largest expression is \(n^2\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Computing a term of a geometric sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute a requested term from the first term and common ratio of a geometric sequence.
questions.question: A geometric sequence has \(a_1=6\) and common ratio \(4\). What is \(a_{4}\)?
questions.explanation: The first term is multiplied by the common ratio \(3\) times to reach term \(4\): \(a_{4}=6\cdot 4^{3}=384\).
questions.hint: The exponent is one less than the index of the requested term.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for binary search
questions.learningObjective: Count worst-case key-to-element comparisons in a specified standard binary-search implementation.
questions.question: Standard binary search examines a sorted array of \(n=9\) distinct elements. It uses an inclusive index interval, chooses the lower middle index, and removes the middle element after an unequal comparison. Count one three-way key-to-element comparison per examined element; exclude index and loop-condition checks. What is the maximum number of these comparisons over all present or absent targets?
questions.explanation: The worst remaining interval after one comparison has \(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor\) elements. Hence \(C(0)=0\) and \(C(n)=1+C(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor)\) for \(n\ge 1\). Repeated halving until the interval is empty gives \(C(n)=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\). For this array, \(C(9)=\lfloor\log_2 9\rfloor+1=4\).
questions.hint: Include the comparison with the final remaining element; stopping when only one candidate remains can miss a comparison.

questions.concept: Summing sequential pipeline stage runtimes
questions.learningObjective: Sum the runtimes of sequential pipeline stages to find total processing time.
questions.question: One item passes through \(4\) sequential pipeline stages taking \(13\), \(7\), \(8\), \(4\) milliseconds, respectively. The item incurs no other delay, and its stages do not overlap. What is its total processing time?
questions.explanation: Add the sequential stage durations: \(13+7+8+4=32\) milliseconds.
questions.hint: The same item completes each stage before starting the next.

questions.concept: Solving a simple additive recurrence by unrolling
questions.learningObjective: Solve a linear recurrence with a fixed additive increment by unrolling it to the base case.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers \(n\), a recurrence satisfies \(T(n)=T(n-1)+6\) for \(n\ge 1\), with \(T(0)=1\). What is \(T(8)\)?
questions.explanation: There are \(8\) steps from the base case, and each adds \(6\). Therefore, \(T(8)=1+8\cdot 6=49\).
questions.hint: Count the steps from the base case and add the increment once per step.

questions.concept: Summing sequential pipeline stage runtimes
questions.learningObjective: Sum the runtimes of sequential pipeline stages to find total processing time.
questions.question: One item passes through \(3\) sequential pipeline stages taking \(22\), \(9\), \(12\) milliseconds, respectively. The item incurs no other delay, and its stages do not overlap. What is its total processing time?
questions.explanation: Add the sequential stage durations: \(22+9+12=43\) milliseconds.
questions.hint: The same item completes each stage before starting the next.

questions.concept: Computing terms of a Fibonacci-style recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Compute terms of a two-term linear recurrence by direct iteration.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers, \(a_0=5\) and \(a_1=2\), while \(a_k=a_{k-1}+a_{k-2}\) for \(k\ge 2\). What is \(a_{5}\)?
questions.explanation:
Build each term from the previous two:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2}&=2+5=7\\
a_{3}&=7+2=9\\
a_{4}&=9+7=16\\
a_{5}&=16+9=25
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(a_{5}=25\).
questions.hint: Start from the two given initial values and compute one new term at a time.

questions.concept: Applying the pigeonhole principle to guarantee a minimum bin size
questions.learningObjective: Apply the pigeonhole principle's ceiling-division bound.
questions.question: \(10\) items are distributed among \(7\) labeled bins. What is the largest integer \(L\) such that every distribution guarantees at least one bin containing \(L\) or more items?
questions.explanation: If every bin held at most \(1\) items, the total would be at most \(7\cdot 1=7\), which is less than \(10\). Therefore some bin has at least \(\left\lceil\frac{10}{7}\right\rceil=2\) items. Distributing the items as evenly as possible attains this largest-bin size, so no stronger guarantee is possible.
questions.hint: Find the ceiling of the average bin size, then check an even distribution to see whether the bound is sharp.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=501\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the smallest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the smallest expression is \(n\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Counting the total number of subsets of a set
questions.learningObjective: Count all subsets by independent inclusion and exclusion choices.
questions.question: How many subsets, including the empty set and the full set, does a set of \(11\) distinct elements have?
questions.explanation: For each element there are two independent choices: include it or exclude it. By the multiplication principle, \(2^{11}=2048\) subsets are possible.
questions.hint: Assign each element one of two inclusion states, then count all state combinations.

questions.concept: Summing sequential pipeline stage runtimes
questions.learningObjective: Sum the runtimes of sequential pipeline stages to find total processing time.
questions.question: One item passes through \(3\) sequential pipeline stages taking \(15\), \(14\), \(13\) milliseconds, respectively. The item incurs no other delay, and its stages do not overlap. What is its total processing time?
questions.explanation: Add the sequential stage durations: \(15+14+13=42\) milliseconds.
questions.hint: The same item completes each stage before starting the next.

questions.concept: Counting leaves in a recursion tree
questions.learningObjective: Count the number of base-case invocations in a recursion tree with a fixed branching factor and depth.
questions.question: The root call is at depth \(0\). Every call at a depth less than \(6\) makes exactly \(3\) child calls, and all calls at depth \(6\) are base cases. How many base-case calls are made?
questions.explanation: The number of calls starts at \(1\) and is multiplied by \(3\) at each depth. At depth \(6\), the leaf count is \(3^{6}=729\).
questions.hint: Count one branching multiplication for each edge-depth between the root and a leaf.

questions.concept: Recovering input size from a linear operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Solve a two-step linear equation to recover an algorithm's input size from a measured operation count.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=8n+7\). One run uses \(151\) operations. What is its nonnegative integer input size \(n\)?
questions.explanation:
Undo the fixed cost, then divide by the coefficient:
\[
\begin{aligned}
8n&=151-7=144\\
n&=\frac{144}{8}=18
\end{aligned}
\]
Checking gives \(8\cdot 18+7=151\).
questions.hint: Remove the fixed overhead before dividing by the per-element cost.

questions.concept: Solving a simple additive recurrence by unrolling
questions.learningObjective: Solve a linear recurrence with a fixed additive increment by unrolling it to the base case.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers \(n\), a recurrence satisfies \(T(n)=T(n-1)+5\) for \(n\ge 1\), with \(T(0)=5\). What is \(T(7)\)?
questions.explanation: There are \(7\) steps from the base case, and each adds \(5\). Therefore, \(T(7)=5+7\cdot 5=40\).
questions.hint: Count the steps from the base case and add the increment once per step.

questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a quadratic time-complexity model with quadratic, linear, and constant terms for a given input size.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=3n^2+n+7\). How many operations are performed when \(n=9\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute and compute the square first:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(9)&=3\cdot 9^2+1\cdot 9+7\\
&=243+9+7=259
\end{aligned}
\]
The count is \(259\) operations.
questions.hint: Square the input size before multiplying by the leading coefficient.

questions.concept: Interpreting an amortized cost bound
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what an amortized per-operation bound implies about total cost over many operations.
questions.question: Starting from an empty dynamic array, a resizing policy guarantees that the total number of element-copy operations over \(65\) insertions is at most \(10\) times the number of insertions. What is the smallest total upper bound supplied by this guarantee alone?
questions.explanation: Apply the given aggregate guarantee: \(10\cdot 65=650\) element-copy operations. This is an upper bound on the entire sequence; an individual insertion may copy more than \(10\) elements.
questions.hint: Apply the stated bound to the entire insertion sequence, rather than to one worst-case insertion.

questions.concept: Counting leaves in a recursion tree
questions.learningObjective: Count the number of base-case invocations in a recursion tree with a fixed branching factor and depth.
questions.question: The root call is at depth \(0\). Every call at a depth less than \(5\) makes exactly \(2\) child calls, and all calls at depth \(5\) are base cases. How many base-case calls are made?
questions.explanation: The number of calls starts at \(1\) and is multiplied by \(2\) at each depth. At depth \(5\), the leaf count is \(2^{5}=32\).
questions.hint: Count one branching multiplication for each edge-depth between the root and a leaf.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on cubic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a cubic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=6n^3\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(7\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?

Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T(7n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{6(7n)^3}{6n^3}\\
&=7^3=343
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(343\).
questions.hint: Substitute the scaled input and form the ratio of the new model to the original.

questions.explanation: Time per item remains fixed, so the new time is \(10\cdot\frac{19}{17}=\frac{190}{17}\) seconds.

questions.concept: Computing throughput from total items and elapsed time
questions.learningObjective: Compute throughput as items processed divided by elapsed time.
questions.question: A pipeline processes \(1560\) transactions in \(30\) seconds at a steady rate. What is its throughput in transactions per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput is the number of processed items divided by elapsed time: \(\frac{1560}{30}=52\) transactions per second.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on quadratic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a quadratic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=3n^2\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(5\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?

Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}

&=5^2=25
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(25\).

questions.concept: Computing amortized per-item cost for a batch operation
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish per-item cost from amortized cost, which spreads the fixed overhead across the whole batch.
questions.question: A batch has a fixed overhead of \(46\) operations and an additional \(6\) operations per item. For a batch of \(46\) items, what is the average number of operations per item? Round the final average to two decimal places when needed.
questions.explanation:
Add the overhead to the total item cost, then average:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{total}&=46+6\cdot 46=322\\
\text{average}&=\frac{322}{46}=7
\end{aligned}
\]
The result is \(7\) operations per item. The fixed overhead is spread across the entire batch.
questions.hint: First find the total batch cost, including overhead; then divide by the number of items.

questions.concept: Counting nodes discovered at a given BFS layer
questions.learningObjective: Count nodes at a given BFS layer in a uniformly branching tree.
questions.question: Breadth-first search explores a rooted tree through layer \(3\). The root is layer \(0\), and every vertex in an earlier layer has exactly \(4\) distinct children. How many vertices are in layer \(3\)?
questions.explanation: A tree gives every child exactly one parent, so no vertices are shared between branches. The layer size is multiplied by \(4\) at each step, giving \(4^{3}=64\) vertices.

questions.concept: Computing throughput from total items and elapsed time
questions.learningObjective: Compute throughput as items processed divided by elapsed time.
questions.question: A pipeline processes \(1960\) tiles in \(20\) seconds at a steady rate. What is its throughput in tiles per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput is the number of processed items divided by elapsed time: \(\frac{1960}{20}=98\) tiles per second.

questions.concept: Computing amortized per-item cost for a batch operation
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish per-item cost from amortized cost, which spreads the fixed overhead across the whole batch.
questions.question: A batch has a fixed overhead of \(20\) operations and an additional \(4\) operations per item. For a batch of \(35\) items, what is the average number of operations per item? Round the final average to two decimal places when needed.
questions.explanation:
Add the overhead to the total item cost, then average:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{total}&=20+4\cdot 35=160\\
\text{average}&=\frac{160}{35}\approx 4.57
\end{aligned}
\]
The result is \(4.57\) operations per item. The fixed overhead is spread across the entire batch.

questions.concept: Applying the handshake lemma to count edges from vertex degrees
questions.learningObjective: Use the handshake lemma on a realizable simple undirected graph.
questions.question: A simple undirected graph has \(8\) vertices with degree sequence \((4,5,7,7,4,5,4,4)\). How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: Each edge contributes one degree at each of its two endpoints. The degree sum is \(4+5+7+7+4+5+4+4=40\), so \(|E|=\frac{40}{2}=20\). The listed sequence has an explicit simple-graph realization, so this degree sum corresponds to a possible graph.
questions.hint: Count how often each edge is included when you add all vertex degrees.

questions.concept: Evaluating a linear operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a linear time-complexity model with a fixed cost and a per-element cost for a given input size.
questions.question: An algorithm has the exact operation-count model \(T(n)=9n+10\). How many operations does it perform when \(n=13\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute the input size: \(T(13)=9\cdot 13+10=127\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply by the per-element coefficient, then add the fixed overhead.

questions.concept: Computing amortized per-item cost for a batch operation
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish per-item cost from amortized cost, which spreads the fixed overhead across the whole batch.
questions.question: A batch has a fixed overhead of \(22\) operations and an additional \(3\) operations per item. For a batch of \(14\) items, what is the average number of operations per item? Round the final average to two decimal places when needed.
questions.explanation:
Add the overhead to the total item cost, then average:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{total}&=22+3\cdot 14=64\\
\text{average}&=\frac{64}{14}\approx 4.57
\end{aligned}
\]
The result is \(4.57\) operations per item. The fixed overhead is spread across the entire batch.
questions.hint: First find the total batch cost, including overhead; then divide by the number of items.

questions.concept: Counting steps in the Euclidean algorithm
questions.learningObjective: Trace the Euclidean algorithm to count the number of division steps to compute a GCD.
questions.question: Starting with \((151,149)\), run the Euclidean algorithm to compute \(\gcd(151,149)\). Count every remainder-producing division, including the final division whose remainder is zero. How many division steps are required?
questions.explanation:
The divisions are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
151&=1\cdot 149+2\\
149&=74\cdot 2+1\\
2&=2\cdot 1+0
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(3\) divisions, including the final zero-remainder division. The last nonzero remainder (or divisor at termination) is \(1\), the greatest common divisor.
questions.hint: Record one step for each computed remainder, and include the step that produces zero.

questions.concept: Applying a proportional scale factor to a workload
questions.learningObjective: Apply a proportional scale factor directly to a workload quantity.
questions.question: A model's workload is directly proportional to input size. The current workload is \(33\) operations. If the input size is multiplied by \(6\), what is the new workload?
questions.explanation: Direct proportionality applies the same factor to the workload: \(33\cdot 6=198\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply the original workload by the input-size scale factor.

questions.concept: Counting the total number of subsets of a set
questions.learningObjective: Count all subsets by independent inclusion and exclusion choices.
questions.question: How many subsets, including the empty set and the full set, does a set of \(6\) distinct elements have?
questions.explanation: For each element there are two independent choices: include it or exclude it. By the multiplication principle, \(2^{6}=64\) subsets are possible.
questions.hint: Assign each element one of two inclusion states, then count all state combinations.

questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a quadratic time-complexity model with quadratic, linear, and constant terms for a given input size.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=2n^2+6n+8\). How many operations are performed when \(n=3\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute and compute the square first:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(3)&=2\cdot 3^2+6\cdot 3+8\\
&=18+18+8=44
\end{aligned}
\]
The count is \(44\) operations.
questions.hint: Square the input size before multiplying by the leading coefficient.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=5002\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the smallest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the smallest expression is \(n\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Applying the Master Theorem to classify a recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Apply the Master Theorem, including the regularity condition when needed, without rounding critical exponents.
questions.question: For \(n=3^k\) with nonnegative integer \(k\), suppose \(T(1)=1\) and \(T(n)=3T\!\left(\frac{n}{3}\right)+n^2\) for \(n>1\). Which Master Theorem case and tight asymptotic bound apply?
questions.explanation: Because \(3<3^{2}\), \(2>\log_{3}3\). Thus the combine cost is polynomially larger than the critical term. The regularity condition holds: \(a f(\frac{n}{b})=\frac{3}{3^{2}}f(n)\), with \(c=\frac{3}{3^{2}}<1\). Therefore Case \(3\) gives \(T(n)=\Theta(n^2)\).
questions.hint: Compare the branching factor with the shrink factor raised to the combine-cost exponent; for combine-cost dominance, also check regularity.

questions.concept: Counting permutations of a set of distinct items
questions.learningObjective: Recall and apply the factorial formula for counting permutations.
questions.question: An algorithm considers every ordering of \(18\) distinct files. How many orderings are possible?
questions.explanation: There are \(18\) choices for the first position, \(17\) for the next, and so on. The product is \(18!=\prod_{i=1}^{18}i=6402373705728000\).
questions.hint: Use the multiplication principle with one fewer available item at each new position.

questions.concept: Applying a proportional scale factor to a workload
questions.learningObjective: Apply a proportional scale factor directly to a workload quantity.
questions.question: A model's workload is directly proportional to input size. The current workload is \(9\) operations. If the input size is multiplied by \(2\), what is the new workload?
questions.explanation: Direct proportionality applies the same factor to the workload: \(9\cdot 2=18\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply the original workload by the input-size scale factor.

questions.concept: Direct proportional scaling of runtime with workload size
questions.learningObjective: Solve a direct-proportion problem relating processing time to workload size.
questions.question: An algorithm processes \(21\) documents in \(9\) seconds. Its runtime is directly proportional to the number of documents. How long does it take to process \(27\) documents at the same rate?
questions.explanation: Time per item remains fixed, so the new time is \(9\cdot\frac{27}{21}=\frac{81}{7}\) seconds.
questions.hint: Scale the original time by the ratio of the new item count to the original item count.

questions.concept: Computing amortized per-item cost for a batch operation
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish per-item cost from amortized cost, which spreads the fixed overhead across the whole batch.
questions.question: A batch has a fixed overhead of \(33\) operations and an additional \(8\) operations per item. For a batch of \(17\) items, what is the average number of operations per item? Round the final average to two decimal places when needed.
questions.explanation:
Add the overhead to the total item cost, then average:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{total}&=33+8\cdot 17=169\\
\text{average}&=\frac{169}{17}\approx 9.94
\end{aligned}
\]
The result is \(9.94\) operations per item. The fixed overhead is spread across the entire batch.
questions.hint: First find the total batch cost, including overhead; then divide by the number of items.

questions.concept: Evaluating a linear operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a linear time-complexity model with a fixed cost and a per-element cost for a given input size.
questions.question: An algorithm has the exact operation-count model \(T(n)=8n+33\). How many operations does it perform when \(n=25\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute the input size: \(T(25)=8\cdot 25+33=233\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply by the per-element coefficient, then add the fixed overhead.

questions.concept: Solving a simple multiplicative recurrence by unrolling
questions.learningObjective: Solve a linear recurrence with a fixed multiplicative factor by unrolling it to the base case.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers \(n\), \(T(0)=4\) and \(T(n)=3T(n-1)\) for \(n\ge 1\). What is \(T(6)\)?
questions.explanation: Apply the multiplier \(3\) once for each of \(6\) steps: \(T(6)=4\cdot 3^{6}=2916\).
questions.hint: Start with the base value and count one multiplication per recurrence step.

questions.concept: Solving the characteristic equation of a linear recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Solve a quadratic characteristic equation associated with a linear recurrence relation.
questions.question: A linear recurrence has the characteristic equation \(x^2+5x-6=0\). What are its two roots?
questions.explanation:
Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2+5x-6&=(x+6)(x-1)\\
(x+6)(x-1)&=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-6\) and \(x=1\). Their sum is \(-6+1=-5\) and their product is \((-6)(1)=-6\), matching the coefficients.
questions.hint: Find a pair whose sum is the negative of the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

questions.concept: Computing expected trials until first success (geometric distribution)
questions.learningObjective: Compute the expected number of independent trials up to and including the first success.
questions.question: An algorithm succeeds on each attempt independently with the same probability \(p=\frac{1}{7}\). Let \(X\) count all attempts up to and including the first success. What is \(\mathbb{E}[X]\)?
questions.explanation: One attempt is always made. With probability \(1-p\), a failure leaves the same expected number of additional attempts. Thus \(\mathbb{E}[X]=1+(1-p)\mathbb{E}[X]\), which gives \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{1}{p}=7\). The first successful attempt is included.
questions.hint: After a failed attempt, the remaining task has the same distribution as at the start.

questions.concept: Computing a net workload reduction (delta)
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a net change (delta) between two workload measurements, including its direction.
questions.question: Caching reduces a service's operation count from \(781\) to \(598\) operations per request. By how many operations per request does the count decrease?
questions.explanation: The reduction is the original count minus the new count: \(781-598=183\) operations per request. This positive reduction measures the size of the decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the new count from the original count.

questions.concept: Determining whether a number is prime
questions.learningObjective: Determine primality by checking for divisors up to the square root of the number.
questions.question: Which statement correctly classifies the integer \(22\) as prime or composite?

options.label: A
options.text: Prime: its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(22\).

questions.explanation: The number has a nontrivial divisor: \(22=2\cdot 11\). Both factors exceed \(1\), so the number is composite.
questions.hint: Try divisors up to the square root; one nontrivial divisor is enough to prove compositeness.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for linear search
questions.learningObjective: Recall the worst-case comparison count for a linear search over n elements.
questions.question: Linear search checks an unsorted array of \(n=338\) elements one at a time. Count one equality comparison between the target and each examined element. What is the worst-case comparison count when the target may be present or absent?
questions.explanation: If the target is absent, every element must be checked. If it is last, the same number of checks is needed. Thus the maximum is \(n=338\) key-to-element comparisons.
questions.hint: Consider a target that is absent or is the final element checked.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on cubic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a cubic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=7n^3\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(3\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?
questions.explanation:
Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T(3n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{7(3n)^3}{7n^3}\\
&=3^3=27
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(27\).
questions.hint: Substitute the scaled input and form the ratio of the new model to the original.

questions.concept: Counting edges in a complete graph
questions.learningObjective: Count the unordered vertex pairs of a simple undirected complete graph.
questions.question: How many edges are in a simple undirected complete graph with \(n=17\) vertices?
questions.explanation: Each edge joins one unordered pair of distinct vertices. Therefore, \(\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\). Substituting \(n=17\) gives \(\frac{17\cdot 16}{2}=136\).
questions.hint: Count unordered pairs of distinct vertices.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=5003\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the smallest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the smallest expression is \(n\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Solving the characteristic equation of a linear recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Solve a quadratic characteristic equation associated with a linear recurrence relation.
questions.question: A linear recurrence has the characteristic equation \(x^2+5x-36=0\). What are its two roots?
questions.explanation:
Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2+5x-36&=(x+9)(x-4)\\
(x+9)(x-4)&=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-9\) and \(x=4\). Their sum is \(-9+4=-5\) and their product is \((-9)(4)=-36\), matching the coefficients.
questions.hint: Find a pair whose sum is the negative of the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for binary search
questions.learningObjective: Count worst-case key-to-element comparisons in a specified standard binary-search implementation.
questions.question: Standard binary search examines a sorted array of \(n=64\) distinct elements. It uses an inclusive index interval, chooses the lower middle index, and removes the middle element after an unequal comparison. Count one three-way key-to-element comparison per examined element; exclude index and loop-condition checks. What is the maximum number of these comparisons over all present or absent targets?
questions.explanation: The worst remaining interval after one comparison has \(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor\) elements. Hence \(C(0)=0\) and \(C(n)=1+C(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor)\) for \(n\ge 1\). Repeated halving until the interval is empty gives \(C(n)=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\). For this array, \(C(64)=\lfloor\log_2 64\rfloor+1=7\).
questions.hint: Include the comparison with the final remaining element; stopping when only one candidate remains can miss a comparison.

questions.concept: Determining whether a number is prime
questions.learningObjective: Determine primality by checking for divisors up to the square root of the number.
questions.question: Which statement correctly classifies the integer \(95\) as prime or composite?

options.label: B
options.text: Prime: its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(95\).

questions.explanation: The number has a nontrivial divisor: \(95=5\cdot 19\). Both factors exceed \(1\), so the number is composite.
questions.hint: Try divisors up to the square root; one nontrivial divisor is enough to prove compositeness.

questions.concept: Identifying the complexity class of a quadratic model
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tight asymptotic class of a quadratic operation-count model.
questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=4n^2+8n+17\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n^2}=4+\frac{8}{n}+\frac{17}{n^2}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(4\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n^2)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.
questions.hint: Identify the highest power with a nonzero positive coefficient.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for linear search
questions.learningObjective: Recall the worst-case comparison count for a linear search over n elements.
questions.question: Linear search checks an unsorted array of \(n=138\) elements one at a time. Count one equality comparison between the target and each examined element. What is the worst-case comparison count when the target may be present or absent?
questions.explanation: If the target is absent, every element must be checked. If it is last, the same number of checks is needed. Thus the maximum is \(n=138\) key-to-element comparisons.
questions.hint: Consider a target that is absent or is the final element checked.

questions.concept: Computing a basic probability as favorable over total outcomes
questions.learningObjective: Apply the basic probability formula: favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
questions.question: A test harness chooses one case uniformly at random from \(22\) cases, of which \(12\) fail. What is the probability of choosing a failing case?
questions.explanation: All cases are equally likely, so \(P(\text{failure})=\frac{12}{22}=\frac{6}{11}\).
questions.hint: Use the number of failing cases divided by the total number of cases.

questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a quadratic time-complexity model with quadratic, linear, and constant terms for a given input size.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=3n^2+n+9\). How many operations are performed when \(n=5\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute and compute the square first:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(5)&=3\cdot 5^2+1\cdot 5+9\\
&=75+5+9=89
\end{aligned}
\]
The count is \(89\) operations.
questions.hint: Square the input size before multiplying by the leading coefficient.

questions.concept: Computing a net workload reduction (delta)
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a net change (delta) between two workload measurements, including its direction.
questions.question: Caching reduces a service's operation count from \(586\) to \(117\) operations per request. By how many operations per request does the count decrease?
questions.explanation: The reduction is the original count minus the new count: \(586-117=469\) operations per request. This positive reduction measures the size of the decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the new count from the original count.

questions.concept: Bounding the length of a shortest simple path
questions.learningObjective: Prove and attain the largest possible shortest-path distance in a simple connected unweighted graph.
questions.question: Consider all simple connected undirected unweighted graphs on \(n=10\) vertices and all pairs of distinct vertices in them. What is the largest possible shortest-path length, measured in edges?
questions.explanation: A shortest path cannot repeat a vertex: removing a cycle would shorten it. It therefore visits at most \(10\) vertices and uses at most \(n-1=9\) edges. This bound is achieved by the two endpoints of a path graph on \(10\) vertices, so it is the largest possible value.
questions.hint: Use the no-repeated-vertex bound, then consider the endpoints of a graph that is itself a path.

questions.concept: Computing a term of a geometric sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute a requested term from the first term and common ratio of a geometric sequence.
questions.question: A geometric sequence has \(a_1=3\) and common ratio \(2\). What is \(a_{5}\)?
questions.explanation: The first term is multiplied by the common ratio \(4\) times to reach term \(5\): \(a_{5}=3\cdot 2^{4}=48\).
questions.hint: The exponent is one less than the index of the requested term.

questions.concept: Evaluating a linear operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a linear time-complexity model with a fixed cost and a per-element cost for a given input size.
questions.question: An algorithm has the exact operation-count model \(T(n)=3n+17\). How many operations does it perform when \(n=18\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute the input size: \(T(18)=3\cdot 18+17=71\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply by the per-element coefficient, then add the fixed overhead.

questions.concept: Computing a value modulo m for hash bucket assignment
questions.learningObjective: Apply the modulo operation to compute a hash bucket index.
questions.question: A hash table assigns key \(75\) to bucket \(75\bmod 12\). What is the bucket index, using remainders from \(0\) through \(11\)?
questions.explanation: Euclidean division gives \(75=12\cdot 6+3\). Since \(0\le 3<12\), the remainder and bucket index are \(3\).
questions.hint: Use the remainder, rather than the quotient, after division by the bucket count.

questions.concept: Computing a runtime after a percentage reduction
questions.learningObjective: Apply a percentage decrease to a runtime value.
questions.question: An optimization reduces a routine's runtime of \(121\) milliseconds by \(20\%\). What is the exact new runtime?
questions.explanation:
Apply the percentage exactly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{reduction}&=121\cdot\frac{20}{100}=24.2\\
\text{new runtime}&=121-24.2=96.8
\end{aligned}
\]
The new runtime is \(96.8\) milliseconds; no integer rounding is applied.
questions.hint: Multiply the original runtime by the fraction that remains after the reduction.

questions.concept: Computing a runtime after a percentage reduction
questions.learningObjective: Apply a percentage decrease to a runtime value.
questions.question: An optimization reduces a routine's runtime of \(67\) milliseconds by \(10\%\). What is the exact new runtime?
questions.explanation:
Apply the percentage exactly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{reduction}&=67\cdot\frac{10}{100}=6.7\\
\text{new runtime}&=67-6.7=60.3
\end{aligned}
\]
The new runtime is \(60.3\) milliseconds; no integer rounding is applied.
questions.hint: Multiply the original runtime by the fraction that remains after the reduction.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on quadratic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a quadratic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=7n^2\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(2\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?
questions.explanation:
Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T(2n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{7(2n)^2}{7n^2}\\
&=2^2=4
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(4\).
questions.hint: Substitute the scaled input and form the ratio of the new model to the original.

questions.concept: Applying a proportional scale factor to a workload
questions.learningObjective: Apply a proportional scale factor directly to a workload quantity.
questions.question: A model's workload is directly proportional to input size. The current workload is \(15\) operations. If the input size is multiplied by \(4\), what is the new workload?
questions.explanation: Direct proportionality applies the same factor to the workload: \(15\cdot 4=60\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply the original workload by the input-size scale factor.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on cubic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a cubic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=6n^3\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(2\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?

Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T(2n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{6(2n)^3}{6n^3}\\
&=2^3=8
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(8\).
questions.hint: Substitute the scaled input and form the ratio of the new model to the original.

questions.concept: Solving the characteristic equation of a linear recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Solve a quadratic characteristic equation associated with a linear recurrence relation.
questions.question: A linear recurrence has the characteristic equation \(x^2-4x-5=0\). What are its two roots?
questions.explanation:
Factor the polynomial, then set each factor equal to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2-4x-5&=(x+1)(x-5)\\
(x+1)(x-5)&=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the roots are \(x=-1\) and \(x=5\). Their sum is \(-1+5=4\) and their product is \((-1)(5)=-5\), matching the coefficients.
questions.hint: Find a pair whose sum is the negative of the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes (largest case)
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=1000\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the largest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the largest expression is \(n^2\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Recovering input size from a linear operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Solve a two-step linear equation to recover an algorithm's input size from a measured operation count.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=9n+20\). One run uses \(290\) operations. What is its nonnegative integer input size \(n\)?
questions.explanation:
Undo the fixed cost, then divide by the coefficient:
\[
\begin{aligned}
9n&=290-20=270\\
n&=\frac{270}{9}=30
\end{aligned}
\]
Checking gives \(9\cdot 30+20=290\).
questions.hint: Remove the fixed overhead before dividing by the per-element cost.

questions.concept: Interpreting an amortized cost bound
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what an amortized per-operation bound implies about total cost over many operations.
questions.question: Starting from an empty dynamic array, a resizing policy guarantees that the total number of element-copy operations over \(25\) insertions is at most \(5\) times the number of insertions. What is the smallest total upper bound supplied by this guarantee alone?
questions.explanation: Apply the given aggregate guarantee: \(5\cdot 25=125\) element-copy operations. This is an upper bound on the entire sequence; an individual insertion may copy more than \(5\) elements.
questions.hint: Apply the stated bound to the entire insertion sequence, rather than to one worst-case insertion.

questions.concept: Counting steps in the Euclidean algorithm
questions.learningObjective: Trace the Euclidean algorithm to count the number of division steps to compute a GCD.
questions.question: Starting with \((163,26)\), run the Euclidean algorithm to compute \(\gcd(163,26)\). Count every remainder-producing division, including the final division whose remainder is zero. How many division steps are required?
questions.explanation:
The divisions are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
163&=6\cdot 26+7\\
26&=3\cdot 7+5\\
7&=1\cdot 5+2\\
5&=2\cdot 2+1\\
2&=2\cdot 1+0
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(5\) divisions, including the final zero-remainder division. The last nonzero remainder (or divisor at termination) is \(1\), the greatest common divisor.
questions.hint: Record one step for each computed remainder, and include the step that produces zero.

questions.concept: Computing amortized per-item cost for a batch operation
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish per-item cost from amortized cost, which spreads the fixed overhead across the whole batch.
questions.question: A batch has a fixed overhead of \(10\) operations and an additional \(5\) operations per item. For a batch of \(26\) items, what is the average number of operations per item? Round the final average to two decimal places when needed.
questions.explanation:
Add the overhead to the total item cost, then average:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{total}&=10+5\cdot 26=140\\
\text{average}&=\frac{140}{26}\approx 5.38
\end{aligned}
\]
The result is \(5.38\) operations per item. The fixed overhead is spread across the entire batch.
questions.hint: First find the total batch cost, including overhead; then divide by the number of items.

questions.concept: Applying the handshake lemma to count edges from vertex degrees
questions.learningObjective: Use the handshake lemma on a realizable simple undirected graph.
questions.question: A simple undirected graph has \(10\) vertices with degree sequence \((7,5,6,6,6,2,5,5,5,1)\). How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: Each edge contributes one degree at each of its two endpoints. The degree sum is \(7+5+6+6+6+2+5+5+5+1=48\), so \(|E|=\frac{48}{2}=24\). The listed sequence has an explicit simple-graph realization, so this degree sum corresponds to a possible graph.
questions.hint: Count how often each edge is included when you add all vertex degrees.

questions.concept: Counting steps in the Euclidean algorithm
questions.learningObjective: Trace the Euclidean algorithm to count the number of division steps to compute a GCD.
questions.question: Starting with \((155,73)\), run the Euclidean algorithm to compute \(\gcd(155,73)\). Count every remainder-producing division, including the final division whose remainder is zero. How many division steps are required?
questions.explanation:
The divisions are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
155&=2\cdot 73+9\\
73&=8\cdot 9+1\\
9&=9\cdot 1+0
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(3\) divisions, including the final zero-remainder division. The last nonzero remainder (or divisor at termination) is \(1\), the greatest common divisor.
questions.hint: Record one step for each computed remainder, and include the step that produces zero.

questions.concept: Computing a net workload reduction (delta)
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a net change (delta) between two workload measurements, including its direction.
questions.question: Caching reduces a service's operation count from \(374\) to \(207\) operations per request. By how many operations per request does the count decrease?
questions.explanation: The reduction is the original count minus the new count: \(374-207=167\) operations per request. This positive reduction measures the size of the decrease.
questions.hint: Subtract the new count from the original count.

questions.concept: Interpreting an amortized cost bound
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what an amortized per-operation bound implies about total cost over many operations.
questions.question: Starting from an empty dynamic array, a resizing policy guarantees that the total number of element-copy operations over \(62\) insertions is at most \(6\) times the number of insertions. What is the smallest total upper bound supplied by this guarantee alone?
questions.explanation: Apply the given aggregate guarantee: \(6\cdot 62=372\) element-copy operations. This is an upper bound on the entire sequence; an individual insertion may copy more than \(6\) elements.
questions.hint: Apply the stated bound to the entire insertion sequence, rather than to one worst-case insertion.

questions.concept: Expressing a workload change as a signed delta
questions.learningObjective: Correctly interpret a negative signed delta as a decrease, distinct from a negative operation count.
questions.question: A refactor changes a function's operation count from \(175\) to \(126\) operations per call. Define the signed change as \(\Delta=\text{new}-\text{original}\). What is \(\Delta\)?
questions.explanation: Using the specified sign convention, \(\Delta=126-175=-49\) operations per call. The negative sign denotes a decrease; the new operation count itself is \(126\) and remains nonnegative.
questions.hint: Use the stated order of subtraction, and let the sign show the direction of change.

questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a quadratic time-complexity model with quadratic, linear, and constant terms for a given input size.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=2n^2+2n+12\). How many operations are performed when \(n=8\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute and compute the square first:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(8)&=2\cdot 8^2+2\cdot 8+12\\
&=128+16+12=156
\end{aligned}
\]
The count is \(156\) operations.
questions.hint: Square the input size before multiplying by the leading coefficient.

questions.concept: Computing total base-case work across a recursion tree
questions.learningObjective: Combine subproblem count and per-subproblem cost to find total work at the base-case level.
questions.question: A divide-and-conquer algorithm starts with input size \(n=32\). Each non-base call makes \(2\) recursive calls on inputs of half its size. The root is depth \(0\), and all calls reach the base case at depth \(5\), with input size \(1\). Each base-case call performs \(9\) operations. How many operations are performed by all base-case calls combined?
questions.explanation: Each branching level multiplies the number of calls by \(2\). Thus there are \(2^{5}=32\) leaves, and their combined work is \(32\cdot 9=288\) operations.
questions.hint: Count the leaves first, then multiply by the work done at each leaf.

questions.concept: Computing expected trials until first success (geometric distribution)
questions.learningObjective: Compute the expected number of independent trials up to and including the first success.
questions.question: An algorithm succeeds on each attempt independently with the same probability \(p=\frac{1}{5}\). Let \(X\) count all attempts up to and including the first success. What is \(\mathbb{E}[X]\)?
questions.explanation: One attempt is always made. With probability \(1-p\), a failure leaves the same expected number of additional attempts. Thus \(\mathbb{E}[X]=1+(1-p)\mathbb{E}[X]\), which gives \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{1}{p}=5\). The first successful attempt is included.
questions.hint: After a failed attempt, the remaining task has the same distribution as at the start.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes (largest case)
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=100002\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the largest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the largest expression is \(n^2\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Determining whether a number is prime
questions.learningObjective: Determine primality by checking for divisors up to the square root of the number.
questions.question: Which statement correctly classifies the integer \(93\) as prime or composite?

options.label: B
options.text: Prime: its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(93\).

questions.explanation: The number has a nontrivial divisor: \(93=3\cdot 31\). Both factors exceed \(1\), so the number is composite.
questions.hint: Try divisors up to the square root; one nontrivial divisor is enough to prove compositeness.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes (largest case)
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=100003\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the largest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the largest expression is \(n^2\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Bounding the length of a shortest simple path
questions.learningObjective: Prove and attain the largest possible shortest-path distance in a simple connected unweighted graph.
questions.question: Consider all simple connected undirected unweighted graphs on \(n=14\) vertices and all pairs of distinct vertices in them. What is the largest possible shortest-path length, measured in edges?
questions.explanation: A shortest path cannot repeat a vertex: removing a cycle would shorten it. It therefore visits at most \(14\) vertices and uses at most \(n-1=13\) edges. This bound is achieved by the two endpoints of a path graph on \(14\) vertices, so it is the largest possible value.
questions.hint: Use the no-repeated-vertex bound, then consider the endpoints of a graph that is itself a path.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on cubic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a cubic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=3n^3\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(6\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?
questions.explanation:
Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T(6n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{3(6n)^3}{3n^3}\\
&=6^3=216
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(216\).
questions.hint: Substitute the scaled input and form the ratio of the new model to the original.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=100002\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the smallest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the smallest expression is \(n\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Identifying the complexity class of a linear model
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tight asymptotic class of a linear operation-count model.
questions.question: For positive integer input sizes \(n\), which tight asymptotic class describes \(T(n)=3n+16\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
questions.explanation: Dividing by the highest power gives \(\frac{T(n)}{n}=3+\frac{16}{n}\). The ratio tends to the positive constant \(3\), so \(T(n)=\Theta(n)\). Big-O alone also permits looser upper bounds; the question asks for a tight class.
questions.hint: Identify the highest power with a nonzero positive coefficient.

questions.concept: Direct proportional scaling of runtime with workload size
questions.learningObjective: Solve a direct-proportion problem relating processing time to workload size.
questions.question: An algorithm processes \(29\) documents in \(14\) milliseconds. Its runtime is directly proportional to the number of documents. How long does it take to process \(26\) documents at the same rate?
questions.explanation: Time per item remains fixed, so the new time is \(14\cdot\frac{26}{29}=\frac{364}{29}\) milliseconds.
questions.hint: Scale the original time by the ratio of the new item count to the original item count.

questions.concept: Computing terms of a Fibonacci-style recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Compute terms of a two-term linear recurrence by direct iteration.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers, \(a_0=4\) and \(a_1=5\), while \(a_k=a_{k-1}+a_{k-2}\) for \(k\ge 2\). What is \(a_{4}\)?
questions.explanation:
Build each term from the previous two:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2}&=5+4=9\\
a_{3}&=9+5=14\\
a_{4}&=14+9=23
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(a_{4}=23\).
questions.hint: Start from the two given initial values and compute one new term at a time.

questions.concept: Solving a simple multiplicative recurrence by unrolling
questions.learningObjective: Solve a linear recurrence with a fixed multiplicative factor by unrolling it to the base case.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers \(n\), \(T(0)=1\) and \(T(n)=2T(n-1)\) for \(n\ge 1\). What is \(T(6)\)?
questions.explanation: Apply the multiplier \(2\) once for each of \(6\) steps: \(T(6)=1\cdot 2^{6}=64\).
questions.hint: Start with the base value and count one multiplication per recurrence step.

questions.concept: Computing throughput from total items and elapsed time
questions.learningObjective: Compute throughput as items processed divided by elapsed time.
questions.question: A pipeline processes \(1376\) documents in \(32\) seconds at a steady rate. What is its throughput in documents per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput is the number of processed items divided by elapsed time: \(\frac{1376}{32}=43\) documents per second.
questions.hint: Divide the total number of processed items by the elapsed time.

questions.concept: Applying the tree edge-count property
questions.learningObjective: Use the edge-count property of a finite tree.
questions.question: A spanning tree connects \(n=96\) vertices of a connected undirected network. How many edges does the tree contain?
questions.explanation: A tree with \(n\) vertices has exactly \(n-1\) edges. Starting with one root, each of the remaining vertices adds one edge to its parent. Here, \(96-1=95\).
questions.hint: In a tree, each vertex other than the root has one edge to its parent.

questions.concept: Solving a simple additive recurrence by unrolling
questions.learningObjective: Solve a linear recurrence with a fixed additive increment by unrolling it to the base case.
questions.question: For nonnegative integers \(n\), a recurrence satisfies \(T(n)=T(n-1)+2\) for \(n\ge 1\), with \(T(0)=3\). What is \(T(9)\)?
questions.explanation: There are \(9\) steps from the base case, and each adds \(2\). Therefore, \(T(9)=3+9\cdot 2=21\).
questions.hint: Count the steps from the base case and add the increment once per step.

questions.concept: Counting permutations of a set of distinct items
questions.learningObjective: Recall and apply the factorial formula for counting permutations.
questions.question: An algorithm considers every ordering of \(19\) distinct jobs. How many orderings are possible?
questions.explanation: There are \(19\) choices for the first position, \(18\) for the next, and so on. The product is \(19!=\prod_{i=1}^{19}i=121645100408832000\).
questions.hint: Use the multiplication principle with one fewer available item at each new position.

questions.concept: Counting combinations (unordered selections)
questions.learningObjective: Count unordered selections without replacement using combinations.
questions.question: A test suite chooses \(2\) distinct test cases from \(8\) available cases without replacement. Order does not matter. How many selections are possible?
questions.explanation: Count ordered choices, then remove the order of the selected group: \(\binom{8}{2}=\frac{8!}{2!(8-2)!}=28\).
questions.hint: Use unordered selections; each selected group has multiple orderings that should be counted only once.

questions.concept: Solving a shared-workload equation with algebraic fractions
questions.learningObjective: Clear algebraic fractions to solve for a total workload split across two processes.
questions.question: A workload contains \(n\) items. In one round, two processes handle disjoint parts: the first processes \(\frac{n}{5}\) items and the second processes \(\frac{n}{2}\) items. Together they process \(35\) items in that round; the rest remain for later. What is the total workload \(n\)?
questions.explanation:
Add the two disjoint processed parts:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{n}{5}+\frac{n}{2}&=35\\
7n&=350\\
n&=50
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution gives \(10\) items for the first process and \(25\) for the second, totaling \(35\).
questions.hint: Add the two fractional portions, then clear the denominators.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for linear search
questions.learningObjective: Recall the worst-case comparison count for a linear search over n elements.
questions.question: Linear search checks an unsorted array of \(n=476\) elements one at a time. Count one equality comparison between the target and each examined element. What is the worst-case comparison count when the target may be present or absent?
questions.explanation: If the target is absent, every element must be checked. If it is last, the same number of checks is needed. Thus the maximum is \(n=476\) key-to-element comparisons.
questions.hint: Consider a target that is absent or is the final element checked.

questions.concept: Effect of scaling input size on cubic runtime
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a cubic operation count scales when the input size is multiplied by a constant factor.
questions.question: An exact operation-count model is \(T(n)=3n^3\) for positive \(n\). If the input size is multiplied by \(7\), by what factor is the operation count multiplied?
questions.explanation:
Compare the new count with the original:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T(7n)}{T(n)}&=\frac{3(7n)^3}{3n^3}\\
&=7^3=343
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient cancels, so the multiplier is \(343\).
questions.hint: Substitute the scaled input and form the ratio of the new model to the original.

questions.concept: Evaluating a linear operation-count model
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a linear time-complexity model with a fixed cost and a per-element cost for a given input size.
questions.question: An algorithm has the exact operation-count model \(T(n)=2n+39\). How many operations does it perform when \(n=3\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute the input size: \(T(3)=2\cdot 3+39=45\) operations.
questions.hint: Multiply by the per-element coefficient, then add the fixed overhead.

questions.concept: Counting subproblems at a given recursion level
questions.learningObjective: Determine how many subproblems exist at a given level of a divide-and-conquer recursion tree.
questions.question: A divide-and-conquer algorithm begins with size \(n=243\). Every call with input size greater than \(1\) makes exactly \(3\) calls, each on an input whose size is divided by \(3\). The root is level \(0\). How many calls are at level \(4\)?
questions.explanation: The input size at level \(4\) is \(\frac{243}{3^{4}}=3\), so the tree reaches this level before the base case. Each earlier level multiplies the call count by \(3\), giving \(3^{4}=81\) calls.
questions.hint: Track the branching factor separately from the factor by which input sizes shrink.

questions.concept: Interpreting an amortized cost bound
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what an amortized per-operation bound implies about total cost over many operations.
questions.question: Starting from an empty dynamic array, a resizing policy guarantees that the total number of element-copy operations over \(37\) insertions is at most \(7\) times the number of insertions. What is the smallest total upper bound supplied by this guarantee alone?
questions.explanation: Apply the given aggregate guarantee: \(7\cdot 37=259\) element-copy operations. This is an upper bound on the entire sequence; an individual insertion may copy more than \(7\) elements.
questions.hint: Apply the stated bound to the entire insertion sequence, rather than to one worst-case insertion.

questions.concept: Comparing the growth of common complexity classes
questions.learningObjective: Understand the relative ordering of common asymptotic growth rates.
questions.question: At input size \(n=10001\), which of the three exact operation-count expressions has the smallest value? All logarithms in the options have base \(2\).
questions.explanation: For this input, \(1<\log_2 n<n\). Multiplying by positive \(n\) gives \(n<n\log_2 n<n^2\). Therefore the smallest expression is \(n\).
questions.hint: Compare each expression after dividing by the positive input size.

questions.concept: Worst-case comparison count for binary search
questions.learningObjective: Count worst-case key-to-element comparisons in a specified standard binary-search implementation.
questions.question: Standard binary search examines a sorted array of \(n=256\) distinct elements. It uses an inclusive index interval, chooses the lower middle index, and removes the middle element after an unequal comparison. Count one three-way key-to-element comparison per examined element; exclude index and loop-condition checks. What is the maximum number of these comparisons over all present or absent targets?
questions.explanation: The worst remaining interval after one comparison has \(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor\) elements. Hence \(C(0)=0\) and \(C(n)=1+C(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor)\) for \(n\ge 1\). Repeated halving until the interval is empty gives \(C(n)=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\). For this array, \(C(256)=\lfloor\log_2 256\rfloor+1=9\).
questions.hint: Include the comparison with the final remaining element; stopping when only one candidate remains can miss a comparison.

questions.concept: Computing a basic probability as favorable over total outcomes
questions.learningObjective: Apply the basic probability formula: favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
questions.question: A test harness chooses one case uniformly at random from \(34\) cases, of which \(16\) fail. What is the probability of choosing a failing case?
questions.explanation: All cases are equally likely, so \(P(\text{failure})=\frac{16}{34}=\frac{8}{17}\).
questions.hint: Use the number of failing cases divided by the total number of cases.
